chapters: In the beginning, God sparked the earth and sky, Void and dark, the waters deep, Spirit hovered high.
God spoke, "Let there be light," and light broke through, Saw it was good, split the night from day, pure and true.
Named the light "day," darkness "night," thus began the sun's sway, Evening to morning, wrapped up the first day.
"Let there be a vault in waters," God declared, so bright, Split the waters, high and low—He called the expanse "sky."
Evening came and morning too, the second day did fly.
To the waters God turned, "Gather up, land appear," Called the land "earth," the seas "seas," everything clear.
"Let the earth sprout green," He commanded with might, Herbs, seeds, fruit-bearing trees, all took flight.
Earth obeyed, green spread wide, and God saw the sight, Evening to morning, completed the third day's light.
"Let there be lights up high," God said with a plan, "Mark seasons, days, years, like only stars can."
Two great lights, sun and moon, stars scattered wide, To shine on earth, rule day and night, side by side.
Evening came, morning followed, fourth day in stride.
Waters teemed with life, birds took to the sky, Great creatures and every winged thing, by His design did fly.
"Be fruitful, multiply!" God blessed sea and air, Evening to morning, the fifth day’s fare.
"Let earth bring forth creatures, each after their kind," Livestock and creeping things, God had in mind.
Then He said, "In our image, let’s create man," "Rule fish, birds, beasts, and the land," was His plan.
Male and female, He created, His blessing came next, "Be fruitful, reign over earth," His words direct.
Every seed and fruit He offered for food, To every creature, His provision was good.
God saw all He had made, and it was very good, Evening to morning, closed the sixth day’s brood.
He made the heavens and the earth, all complete, On the seventh day, God took a seat. He finished His work, sat back and rested, That seventh day, He blessed and invested.
In history's tale, creation's debut, No plants or herbs, no rain but dew. No man to till, just mist on the ground, Then God shaped man from dust all around.
He breathed life in, made man stand tall, A living soul, the first of them all. In Eden's garden, eastward He placed, The man He formed, with love embraced.
Trees grew lush, a sight to behold, With fruit for food, and stories untold. A river flowed, to water the land, Split into four, by God's own hand.
Pishon first, through Havilah it streams, Where gold and stones fulfill rich dreams. Gihon next, through Cush it winds, Hiddekel flows where Assyria finds.
The fourth, the Euphrates, vast and wide, In Eden's garden, man did abide. "Eat freely," God said, "of every tree, But not that one, or die you'll see."
God saw man alone, not good to be, "A helper I'll make, comparable to thee." From earth, beasts and birds came alive, To man they came, names to derive.
Man named the creatures, one by one, But no partner found, none under the sun. A deep sleep fell, God took a rib, From that rib, a woman He did give.
"Bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh," Man saw woman, love did refresh. Man leaves his kin, to join his wife, Together as one, they start their life.
Naked they stood, no shame to bear, Together in Eden, a perfect pair.
The serpent was sly, more subtle than the rest, He asked the woman, "God said you can't eat, is that the test?"
The woman replied, "We can eat from the trees all around, But that one in the middle, touch it, and we're ground-bound."
The serpent whispered, "You won’t really die, God knows if you eat, you'll see with His eye."
She saw that the tree had a delightful taste, Took the fruit, ate it, not a moment to waste.
Gave some to her man, and he ate too, Their eyes popped open, they knew what was true.
They realized their nakedness, quick with a sew, Fig leaves fashioned, the first clothes they’d know.
God's steps echoed in the cool evening air, They hid in the garden, trembling in despair.
"Where are you?" called God with a voice deep and grand, "I heard you, got scared; I'm naked," said the man.
"Who told you that truth you now bear? Did you eat from that tree over there?"
The man pointed, "The woman, you gave her to me, She handed the fruit, and I ate from the tree."
God asked the woman, "Why did you do this deed?" "The serpent deceived, it planted the seed."
God turned to the snake, "For this trick you played, Cursed above all, on your belly you’ll stay.
Between you and the woman, a battle will rage, Her offspring will crush you, head and heel engaged."
To the woman He said, "In childbirth, much pain, Your desire for your man, in your heart he'll reign."
To Adam He spoke of labor's tough call, "You listened to your wife, now the ground’s a thrall.
Thorns and thistles, the land will churn, By sweat you’ll eat, till dust you return."
The man named her Eve, life's mother, it's clear, God made them garments, to cover their fear.
"Behold, man is like us, knowing both good and ill, Lest he eat from the tree of life, forever still."
So out from Eden, God sent them away, To toil the ground, where man was of clay.
Guarding the garden, cherubim stood, A flaming sword, turning every way it could.
In the beginning, Eve knew her man, and birthed Cain, With Yahweh's touch, their family was gained.
Next came Abel, keeper of the sheep, While Cain tilled the ground, his harvest to reap.
Time rolled on, offerings were made, Cain brought fruits, while Abel's flock was displayed.
God favored Abel, Cain's face fell in pain, "Why you angry?" God asked, "Why the disdain?"
"Do well, lift up; sin's at your door, Desire's for you, but rule it, for sure."
Cain whispered to Abel, "Let's head to the field," There brother turned against brother, and Abel was killed.
"Where's Abel?" God asked, Cain played coy, "Am I his keeper, or his decoy?"
"What have you done?" the blood cries out, Now cursed from the ground, no more will it sprout.
Fugitive, wanderer, cursed by the earth, Cain cried, "Too great, this punishment's worth!"
God marked Cain with a protective sign, "No one will harm you, vengeance is mine."
Cain left, settled East of Eden's gate, To Nod he went, to face his fate.
Cain’s line grew, Enoch was born, A city he built, legacy adorned.
Then came Lamech, with two wives by his side, Adah and Zillah, with stories to bide.
Jabal and Jubal, and Tubal Cain, Crafting, music, and tools they gained.
Lamech's voice echoed, "Hear my claim, Seventy-seven times, vengeance I proclaim."
Adam knew Eve, Seth was her joy, "God replaced Abel, whom Cain destroyed."
Seth had Enosh, calling Yahweh's name began, A new chapter for God's chosen clan.
In the day God made man, His likeness He crafted, Male and female He blessed, His image never shafted. Named them Adam, the first of human creation, He lived long, fathered Seth, his next generation.
Adam clocked nine hundred thirty, then he died, Seth took the baton, Enosh was next in stride. Seth lived nine twelve years, then he laid to rest, Enosh fathered Kenan, in life's eternal quest.
Enosh's days numbered nine hundred and five, Kenan came next, kept the lineage alive. Lived nine hundred ten, then to the earth he returned, Fathered Mahalalel, life's lessons were learned.
Mahalalel lived long, passed the torch to Jared, Eight ninety-five years before he finally perished. Jared birthed Enoch, who walked with God on high, Nine sixty-two years, then he waved goodbye.
Enoch was special, three hundred sixty-five, Walked with God closely, then wasn’t found alive. God took him up, a mystery untold, A legacy divine, a tale to behold.
Methuselah, his son, lived the longest span, Nine sixty-nine years, the life of a wise man. Fathered Lamech, who in time bore a son, Named Noah, "He'll comfort us," the prophecy begun.
Lamech's days were seven seventy-seven, Then went to rest, a foreshadow of heaven. Noah at five hundred, fathered three, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, beginning of history's spree.

People multiplied on the ground, daughters were born, God's sons saw beauty, took wives, the world was torn. Yahweh spoke, "My Spirit won't strive with man, He's flesh, his days numbered to a hundred twenty span."
Nephilim roamed, mighty men of renown, God’s sons and daughters, legends all around. But wickedness grew, man's thoughts were dark, Yahweh grieved deeply, His heart left a mark.
"I'll destroy man," Yahweh declared with regret, "Man and beast, all that I’ve met. I’m sorry I made them," His sorrow was told, But Noah found favor, a story to unfold.
Noah was righteous, blameless in his time, He walked with God, his life a steady rhyme. Three sons he fathered: Shem, Ham, Japheth, But the earth was corrupt, violence was its breath.
God saw the earth, corrupt and vile, "An end to all flesh," He warned with a trial. "Make a ship of gopher wood, rooms inside, Seal it with pitch, let it be your guide.
Its length three hundred, width fifty, thirty tall, Roof it well, door on the side, heed this call. Lower, second, third levels in the ship reside, For a flood comes, waters worldwide."
"Establish my covenant," God promised to Noah, "Enter the ark, you and your kin, stay in the flow-a. Two of each creature, male and female, Birds, beasts, creeps, on your ship they’ll sail.
Gather food, enough for all to survive, Sustain yourselves till new life can thrive." Noah obeyed, did all God ordered, Faithful to the task, his resolve never faltered.
"Get in the ship, Noah, bring your whole clan, I've seen your righteousness across this land.
Seven pairs of the clean, two unclean, male and mate, Birds of the sky, seven and seven, populate.
In seven days, rain will pour, forty nights, forty days, Every living thing washed away in this watery blaze."
Noah did as was told, at Yahweh's command, Six hundred years old when the flood hit the land.
Into the ship, Noah with family walked, Floodwaters rising, none of them balked.
Clean and unclean, birds and beasts did creep, By twos, they entered, no time to sleep.
Seven days passed, floodwaters arrived, Fountains burst open, sky's windows wide.
Forty days of rain, a deluge of might, Noah and kin sheltered from the night.
Every creature, every kind took their place, In the ship, safe from the flood's fierce embrace.
God shut them in, sealed them tight, Waters rose, lifting the ship into flight.
Floodwaters climbed, mountains submerged, All life outside, in the waves, were purged.
Breath of life, stilled in nostrils, all gone, Only Noah and crew lived on at dawn.
For one fifty days, waters covered the land, Noah afloat, saved by God's hand.
Noah and his crew stayed afloat, on the waves they did rely, God blew the wind, and watched as the flood began to die.
Deep’s fountains stopped, sky’s windows closed, rain ceased to fall, Waters pulled back, slowly receding, answering the call.
One fifty days went by, ship found its resting place, Seventh month, seventeenth day, on Ararat it embraced.
Waters kept falling till the tenth month came around, Mountains' tops appeared, rising from the drowned.
Forty days passed, Noah opened the window wide, Sent a raven flying, till water no longer cried.
Next a dove he sent, searching for dry ground, Dove found none, back to Noah's hand she was bound.
Seven days more, another dove was deployed, With evening came an olive leaf, Noah's hope was buoyed.
Another week flew by, dove flew and did not return, Noah knew the earth was dry, life was ready to turn.
Six hundred first year, first month, first day, Noah uncovered, saw the land where water once lay.
By second month’s end, the earth was completely dry, God spoke to Noah, "Time to say goodbye.
"Leave the ark, take your wife, sons, and their wives too, Bring out every creature, let them start anew.
"Let them breed, let them spread, fill the earth wide, Be fruitful, multiply, let life not be denied."
Noah and his family, animals in stride, Exited the ark, feeling the dry land abide.
Noah built an altar, offerings to Yahweh burned, Pleasant aroma rose, God's heart then turned.
He whispered, "No more will I curse the ground for man's sinful start, As long as the earth remains, seasons won't depart."
Seedtime, harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter's sway, Day and night will not cease, they’ll continue their display.
God blessed Noah and his sons with might, "Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth right.
Animals and birds, they'll fear your command, Every creature and fish, delivered to your hand.
Every moving thing will be food, that's true, Like the green herb I gave, everything's for you.
But flesh with blood, don't eat, it's not right, I'll require blood for life, by day or by night.
Whoever sheds blood, theirs will be shed, For man reflects God, in whose image they're bred.
So be fruitful and multiply, roam the earth wide, Increase and fill it, with life on every side."
God spoke to Noah, His voice clear and grand, "My covenant I make, with you and your band.
With your offspring, with creatures, every single one, From the birds to the beasts, under the sun.
Never again shall flood destroy all the earth, This is my promise, a new era's birth.
I set a rainbow, a sign in the cloud, A covenant of peace, forever vowed.
When clouds roll in, and the rainbow shines, I'll remember the promise, through all the times.
The rainbow's a sign, of the bond I’ve sown, Between me and all life, forever known."
Shem, Ham, Japheth stepped from the ship's berth, From these three sons, came the whole earth.
Noah became a farmer, with vineyard first-rate, Drank wine, got drunk, in his tent he laid.
Ham saw his father's state, then spread the tale, But Shem and Japheth walked backward, to prevail.
Covered their father, with respect and care, Faced away, not seeing his bare.
Noah awoke, knew what had been done, Cursed Canaan, Ham's troublesome son.
"Blessed be Yahweh, God of Shem," he cried, "Let Canaan serve, with Japheth by his side.
May God enlarge Japheth, in Shem's tents abide, Let Canaan be servant to brothers worldwide."
Noah lived long, three-fifty more years flew, Nine hundred fifty in all, then he bid adieu.
After the flood, the world began anew, Sons of Noah, their families grew.
Japheth’s sons, Gomer and Magog, to name, Madai, Javan, Tubal, adding to the fame.
Gomer’s kids were Ashkenaz, Riphath, Togarmah, Javan’s line stretched far, to Kittim and Dodanim afar.
Islands and nations split by tongue, Each in their lands, their stories sung.
Ham’s line came with Cush, Mizraim's might, Put, Canaan, spreading in the world’s sight.
Cush’s children like Raamah, Seba stood tall, Nimrod, a mighty hunter, known to all.
"Babel," he built, kingdoms arose, Erech and Accad, where his prowess shows.
Mizraim’s offspring, tribes wide and vast, From Ludim to Philistines, their lineage cast.
Canaan’s legacy, cities spread wide, Sidon to Gaza, where borders abide.
Shem, the elder, his children were led, Elam, Asshur, and Arpachshad bred.
Aram fathered Uz, Hul, Gether, Mash, Eber’s line was Peleg, Joktan in a flash.
Joktan’s sons, Almodad through Jobab's tale, In the east, their lands prevail.
From Mesha to Sephar, mountains high, Shem’s children spread, reaching the sky.
Noah’s sons birthed nations, each a proud story, Divided the earth, in their lands, their glory.

The earth spoke as one, one language, one tone, From the east they traveled, in Shinar they found their home. "Let's make bricks," they said, "burn them good and tight," Building a city and a tower reaching high in the night.
"Come on," they chanted, "let's make a name, So we won't be scattered, lost to fame." But Yahweh came down, took a look at their plan, "One people, one tongue, now it's time to span.
What they start, they’ll complete, nothing will bind, Let's mix up their speech, confuse their mind.” So Yahweh descended, with a twist of His hand, Scattering them far across every land.
Babel it was called, for there speech was tangled, From that place, all nations were dangled. Now, Shem's generations unfold, Two years post-flood, Arpachshad took hold.
Shem lived on, five hundred years more, Sons and daughters he had, a great score. Arpachshad, thirty-five, fathered Shelah in line, Lived four hundred more, with a family fine.
Shelah had Eber, after thirty years passed, Four hundred years more, his legacy amassed. Eber fathered Peleg, at thirty-four years, Then lived many more, with sons and their peers.
Peleg to Reu, thirty was his age, Two hundred years more, his life's full page. Reu had Serug, thirty-two on the clock, Two hundred more years, in life's endless walk.
Serug to Nahor, at thirty he lived, Two hundred more, to his kin he did give. Nahor had Terah after twenty-nine years, One hundred nineteen more, with family cheers.
Terah had Abram, Nahor, and Haran his son, Haran fathered Lot, but life was undone. In Ur of the Chaldees, Haran met his fate, While Terah was living, his life couldn't wait.
Abram wed Sarai, Nahor took Milcah's hand, Sarai was barren, no child to command. Terah took Abram, Lot, and Sarai in tow, From Ur to Canaan, but in Haran they'd slow.
Two hundred five years, Terah's life spanned, And there in Haran, his life did land.
God said to Abram, "Leave your land, your kin, Head to the place where new life will begin. I'll make you a great nation, your name shall rise, A blessing to many, beneath the skies."
"Those who bless you, I'll bless them too, But curse those who treat you with a view askew. All earth's families through you will be blessed," So Abram listened, and he did his best.
At seventy-five, Abram hit the road, With Lot and Sarai, they shared the load. To Canaan they went with all their gear, Entering the land, they had no fear.
Through Shechem's land, to Moreh's oak, Canaanites watched as Yahweh spoke: "I'll give this land to your seed," He said, An altar Abram built, where Yahweh led.
He moved his tent east of Bethel's hill, Called on Yahweh’s name, obeyed His will. Southward he traveled, through the land's breadth, Till famine struck hard, with hunger and death.
Down to Egypt, they journeyed afar, Famine was fierce, no food in the jar. Abram said to Sarai, "You're a beauty, no doubt, When Egyptians see you, they'll figure me out."
"They'll kill me for you, so do this thing, Say you're my sister, and safety we'll bring." In Egypt's gates, Sarai's beauty shone, Praised by princes in Pharaoh's throne.
Pharaoh took her, and Abram gained wealth, With flocks and servants, he thrived in health. But God struck Pharaoh's house with dread, For Sarai's sake, the plagues spread.
Pharaoh called Abram, "What have you done? Why say 'sister,' hiding you're one? Take your wife back, now go your way," Escorted by men, they left that day.
Abram left Egypt, with his wife and Lot so grand, Into the South, with riches, livestock in hand.
His journey took him back to Bethel's holy ground, Where he'd pitched his tent, and Yahweh's name was found.
Lot was there too, with flocks and tents in tow, But the land was too cramped, their wealth began to show.
Herdsmen clashed, their voices raised in heated claim, Canaanites and Perizzites mingled in the same.
Abram spoke to Lot, "Let's not fight, we're kin, Choose your path left or right, so peace can begin."
Lot gazed out, saw the Jordan plain so lush and wide, Before Yahweh's wrath on Sodom's sinful side.
He picked his place, journeyed east, they parted ways, Abram stayed in Canaan, in Yahweh's gaze.
The men of Sodom, wicked, against Yahweh's will, While Abram in Canaan, the promise to fulfill.
Yahweh spoke to Abram, with vision bold and grand, "Look around, all directions, this is your land.
Your offspring countless as the dust beneath your feet, This promise I give, will never know defeat.
Rise, walk the land's length and breadth, see what I bestow, For this land's yours forever, as far as you can go."
Abram settled by Mamre's oaks, in Hebron's embrace, Built an altar to Yahweh, in that holy place.
In the days of kings with lands to claim, In the Valley of Siddim, they played their game.
Chedorlaomer ruled with might, But in thirteen years, the kings took flight.
Four kings rode, rebellion in sight, Struck giants and foes, left them in fright.
The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah made their stand, Against Chedorlaomer’s fierce command.
The valley was slick with tar and doom, Some kings fled, others met their tomb.
Goods of cities were taken away, Along with Lot, in disarray.
One escaped to Abram, told his tale, By Mamre’s oaks, he vowed to prevail.
Three hundred eighteen, his men trained to fight, Pursuing by night, with might and sight.
They struck in the shadows, scattered their foes, Rescued Lot, returned with those.
The king of Sodom met him with relief, Melchizedek came, his words like a chief.
"Bread and wine, a blessing I bring, To Abram, blessed by the Most High King."
"So bless the Almighty, who gave you strength, Delivered your foes at full length."
Abram bowed, gave a tenth to show, His gratitude to Melchizedek’s glow.
The king of Sodom with an offer bold, "Give me the people, keep the gold."
But Abram replied, his vow held high, "To Yahweh I’ve promised, no riches I’ll buy."
"Not a thread nor strap shall I take, For it's the Lord’s name I won’t forsake."
His men’s portions alone he'd let stand, Aner, Eshcol, Mamre, they'd take their hand.
In a vision, God's word came, "Abram, don't fear, I'm your shield, your reward, your fortune's near."
Abram said, "Lord, what will you give me? I'm childless, and Eliezer's all I see."
"No children have come my way, just so you know, A servant's my heir, can't let my legacy go."
God spoke again, "This man won't take the lead, Your heir's your own flesh and bone, indeed."
He led Abram outside, stars filled the night, "Count them if you can, they'll guide your sight."
"Just like these stars, your offspring will be." Abram believed, righteousness given free.
"I am Yahweh, brought you from Ur's land, To give you inheritance, a promise grand."
Abram asked, "Lord, how will I know for sure?" God replied, "Bring me offerings, pure and secure."
A heifer, goat, ram, dove, and pigeon laid down, Abram split them, set them on the ground.
Birds of prey swooped, but Abram stood guard, Chased them away, kept his heart hard.
As the sun set, darkness and fear came, Deep sleep fell, Abram heard God proclaim:
"Your offspring will roam, as strangers they'll serve, Afflicted for years, but wealth they'll deserve."
"I'll judge the nation they’ll serve with toil, But you'll rest in peace, safe in the soil."
Fourth generation, they'll return to this space, Amorite iniquity's not yet full in this place."
Darkness descended, and what did he see? A smoking furnace, torch lit the debris.
That day, God made a covenant so bold, "To your offspring, this land I hold.
From Egypt's river to Euphrates so wide, Kenites to Jebusites, all yours," God confide.
Sarai's heart was heavy, no child in sight, But Hagar was near, an Egyptian in her plight. Sarai spoke to Abram, "See, Yahweh's held me back, Go to my servant, maybe she'll pick up the slack."
Abram nodded, listening to Sarai's plea, He took Hagar as his wife, that's how it'd be. She conceived a child, but trouble brewed, Hagar now looked at Sarai with a different mood.
Sarai went to Abram, "This wrong's on you, I gave her to you, now look at what she's put me through. May Yahweh judge between you and me, For she's despised me, can't you see?"
Abram shrugged, "She's yours to command, Do what feels right, it's in your hand." Sarai dealt harshly, Hagar ran away, To a wilderness fountain, where she'd stay.
Yahweh's angel asked, "Where you from? Where you go?" "I'm fleeing my mistress," she let him know. "Return to her and submit," the angel said, "I'll multiply your offspring, they'll surely spread."
"You're with child, a son you'll bear, Call him Ishmael, for Yahweh heard your despair. A wild donkey he'll be, against every hand, Living apart, in a solitary land."
"You are a God who sees," Hagar proclaimed, By the well Beer Lahai Roi, it was named. Hagar bore a son, Ishmael his name, Abram was eighty-six when his boy came.

When Abram hit ninety-nine, God appeared clear and bright, Said, "I'm God Almighty, walk before me, live right. I'll make my covenant, it's between me and you, I'll multiply you greatly, watch what I do."
Abram hit the ground, face down in awe, God spoke again, laying down the law, "With you my covenant will stand, it's true, Father of nations, that's who you'll be, you."
"No more Abram, Abraham's your new name, Nations and kings from you, they'll proclaim. I'll make you fruitful, more than you know, The land of Canaan, to your offspring, I'll bestow."
God said, "Keep my covenant, you and your kin, Every male circumcised, the sign of what's within. At eight days old, seal the deal on their skin, Born or bought, let the covenant begin."
"Break the covenant? That soul's cast out, In your flesh, my promise, there's no doubt." "For Sarai, call her Sarah, her name's renewed, Mother of nations, through her my promise pursued."
Abraham laughed, "Can I father a child, this old? Will Sarah at ninety, a son behold?" He pleaded for Ishmael, but God was clear, "Sarah will bear Isaac, my promise sincere."
"For Ishmael, I've heard, he'll be great too, Twelve princes will rise, a nation they'll pursue. But with Isaac, my covenant firmly remains, Next year, Sarah's joy, my promise sustains."
God ascended, His words etched in Abraham's mind, Abraham acted, not leaving one behind. Every male in his house, circumcised that day, At ninety-nine, he led, showing the way.
Ishmael at thirteen, joined the obedient line, In Abraham's camp, the covenant's sign. In unity, they stood, God's promise held tight, Circumcised together, in the same daylight.
By the oaks of Mamre, heat of the day, Abraham sat, in the tent he'd stay.
Three men stood near, he lifted his eyes, Ran to greet them, no surprise.
"My lord, if I've found favor, don't depart, Let me bring water, refresh your heart."
"Fetch some bread, take a rest under the tree," "Very well, do as you say," they agreed with glee.
To Sarah he rushed, "Knead some dough, make it quick," Ran to the herd, picked a calf, tender and slick.
Butter, milk, the calf prepared, served with pride, Stood by the tree, as they ate, side by side.
"Where's Sarah, your wife?" they inquired with care, "In the tent," he replied, she was hiding there.
"I'll return next year, Sarah will bear a son," Sarah laughed inside, disbelief had begun.
"I'm old, my lord's old, how can this be?" "Why did Sarah laugh? Nothing's too hard for Me."
Sarah denied, "I didn't laugh," fear in her tone, "No, but you did," Yahweh said, truth like a stone.
Men rose, looked toward Sodom, on they would go, Abraham walked with them, his anxiety wouldn't slow.
"Shall I hide my plans from Abraham, my friend? Through him, all nations will bless, to the end."
"Sodom's cry is great, their sin so dire, I’ll see if the deeds match the reports that inspire."
The men turned to Sodom, but Abraham stayed, "Will the righteous with the wicked be slayed?"
"What if fifty righteous are found in the city?" "For their sake, I'll spare, isn't that a pity?"
"What if five less, only forty-five remain?" "For forty-five, I’ll spare, again and again."
"Don't be angry, Lord, if I say it right, What if only forty are in sight?"
"No destruction for forty," Yahweh replied, "What if thirty?” Abraham cried.
"No harm for thirty," Yahweh did assure, "What if twenty, can you promise me more?"
"For twenty's sake, the city stands strong," "One last time, Lord, don't find me wrong."
"What if ten righteous dwell in this place?" "For ten, I'll spare it, free from disgrace."
Yahweh departed, His words were complete, Abraham returned, his heart in retreat.
Two angels hit Sodom when evening fell, Lot at the gate, knew something to tell. He rose up quick, got on the ground, "Come to my house, stay around."
They said, "Naw, we'll rest on the street," But Lot insisted, so they took a seat. He made a feast, bread without leaven, But Sodom's men brought no heaven.
They gathered 'round, pounding the door, "Bring out the men, we want more." Lot stepped out, shut the door fast, "Don't do this evil, let it pass."
"Take my daughters," Lot did plead, "These men are under my roof, take heed." But they pushed, wanting more, Angels pulled Lot in, slammed the door.
Blinded the crowd, great and small, "Who else you got? We’re saving y’all." "The city's doomed, we’ll make it fall," "Get your kin, save them all."
Lot ran, warned his kin, “Yahweh’s wrath, it’s coming in!" But they laughed, thought it a joke, Judgment wasn't a thing they awoke.
Morning light, angels pressed, "Get your family, flee the mess." Lot lingered, fear took hold, Angels grabbed, mercy bold.
"Escape for life, don’t look back, To the mountains, don’t you slack." Lot begged, "Let’s detour, To a small city, I'll be sure."
Angels agreed, "Hurry there, I’ll spare that place, heed my prayer." Fire fell, sulfur and smoke, Cities fell, earth awoke.
Lot’s wife turned, a salty end, Too late now to comprehend. Smoke rose high, Abraham saw, God’s true judgment, without flaw.
Lot lived mountain-high, Daughters plotted, no men nearby. Wine flowed, plans were laid, Preserve the line, no delay made.
Firstborn, then the young, Lay with their father, songs unsung. Moab and Ben-Ammi born, Two nations from daughters’ scorn.

Abraham moved south, foreign lands he'd explore, Between Kadesh and Shur, he settled in Gerar's core. Called Sarah his sister, not his wife in disguise, Abimelech took her, a king's unexpected surprise.

God showed up in a dream, said, “Behold, you're dead, For the woman's a wife, not a sister,” God said. Abimelech hadn't touched her, he pleaded his case, “Will you slay the righteous, bring guilt to this place?
He called her his sister, she said he's her brother, I acted in innocence, one way or the other.” God answered, “I know, that's why I intervened, Kept you from sinning, unseen but keen.
Now give her back, she's a prophet's wife, He’ll pray for you, restore your life. If you refuse, know that death's your fate, For you and your kingdom, if you hesitate.”
Abimelech rose early, told his servants the tale, Fear spread through the land, faces turned pale. He summoned Abraham, asked, “What have you done? Brought a great sin, no wrong had I begun.”
Abraham confessed, “Thought God’s fear was none, They'd kill me for Sarah, my life would be gone. She’s truly my sister, just not of my mother, A complex truth, but yes, she’s my lover.”
Abimelech gifted sheep, cattle, and more, Restored Sarah to Abraham, peace they swore. “My land is open, live where you please,” To Sarah he said, “Your worth, all will see.”
Abraham prayed, God healed the king's kin, Opened their wombs, new life could begin. For Yahweh had shut them, because of this plight, But now peace restored, all things set right.
God visited Sarah just as He said, And she bore a son when her hope had fled.
Abraham named his boy Isaac, with pride, Circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had prescribed.
Old man Abraham, a hundred, when Isaac arrived, Sarah laughed, said, "Who'd have thought I'd keep this dream alive?"
The child grew and was weaned, a feast set the stage, But Sarah saw Hagar's son mocking, fueled her rage.
She said to Abraham, "Send them away! The servant's child won't share Isaac's day."
Troubled was Abraham, caught in the plight, But God said, "Listen, Isaac's your light.
Yet Hagar's boy, a nation I'll create, For he's your child, his future is great."
Early morning, bread and water in hand, Abraham sent Hagar wandering this land.
In Beersheba's wild, the water ran dry, Hagar wept, couldn't watch her son die.
God heard the boy, sent an angel to say, "Hagar, fear not, I'll show you the way.
Lift up the boy, a great nation he'll be, Open your eyes, a well you will see."
With water renewed, the boy drank with grace, Grew in the wild, an archer he embraced.
Abimelech saw God with Abraham’s might, Asked for truth, a covenant to write.
Abraham agreed, yet complained of a well, Abimelech knew not, swore tales to quell.
Sheep and cattle, a covenant they made, Seven ewe lambs, a witness displayed.
Beersheba named for oaths they swore, Abimelech and Phicol left with a roar.
Abraham planted a tamarisk tree, Called on Yahweh, forever to be.
In Philistine lands, for many days did he dwell, A foreigner living, with stories to tell.
"Abraham!" God called, putting him to the test, "Here I am," said Abe, ready for the quest.
"Take your son, your only one you love so true, To Moriah's land, it's an offering I ask of you."
Early morning rise, with donkey saddled tight, Took two young men, and Isaac, journeying to the height.
Third day dawned, Abe saw the place afar, Told the young men, "Stay here, we'll worship under the star."
Wood on Isaac's back, fire and knife in hand, Together they walked, through desolate land.
Isaac asked, "Father, where's the lamb we need?" "God will provide," Abe said, "trust in His lead."
At the place, the altar built, wood laid in order, Bound Isaac, laid him down, fulfilling the border.
Hand stretched out, knife ready to strike, An angel's voice called, halting the hike.
"Abraham, Abraham!" in the sky it resounded, "Here I am," he answered, his heart astounded.
"Don't touch the boy, for now I truly see, You fear God, withholding nothing from me."
Eyes lifted, a ram caught in the thicket, A substitute offering, God provided the ticket.
"Yahweh Will Provide," Abe named that place, On God's mountain, provision's embrace.
From heaven again, the angel did declare, "By My own name, Abe, you'll be blessed beyond compare.
Your descendants like stars, like sand on the shore, Enemies' gates yours, nations blessed evermore."
Back to his young men, they rose and went on, In Beersheba, Abe's journey carried on.
News came to Abe, Milcah bore sons to Nahor, Uz, Buz, and Aram, new family lore.
Rebekah from Bethuel, the family tree grew, With Gaham and Maacah, to Abraham the news flew.
Sarah lived long, a hundred twenty-seven years, In Hebron, she passed, bringing Abraham to tears.
He rose up, spoke to the Heth crowd, "I’m a stranger here, but I ask proud.
Give me a plot to bury my dead, A place for her, where she can be laid to bed."
The children of Heth replied in grace, "A prince of God, you hold a special place.
Choose any tomb, don't hesitate or dread, None will deny you, bury your dead."
Abraham stood, bowed to the land's folk, He spoke again, respectful was his stroke.
"Let Ephron know, I want his cave, At Machpelah's end, a price I’ll save."
Ephron sat among them, he replied with ease, "My lord, the field and cave, take them, please.
In front of all, this gift is shown, Bury your beloved, make it known."
Abraham bowed, respectful in his plea, "Yet hear me out, let the price be."
Ephron named it, four hundred silver shekels ring, "What's that between us? Let it bring—"
Abraham weighed the silver right, The field and cave now his in sight.
Before all Heth, the deal was made, The land was Abraham's, the price he paid.
There in Machpelah, in Hebron's space, Abraham laid Sarah in her final resting place.
The field and cave, deeded and done, A burial site secured, a legacy begun.
Abraham was old, blessed far and wide, Called his servant close, with a task to confide.
"Put your hand under my thigh, make this vow, Don't seek a wife for Isaac from Canaanites now.
Head to my homeland, where my kin reside, Find a wife for my son, make her his bride."
The servant asked, "What if she won't come here? Should I take Isaac back?" Abraham said, "Hear:
'The God of heaven, who brought me away, Will send His angel, guide your way.
If she won't follow, you're freed from this vow, But don't take Isaac back, not then, not now.'"
The servant swore, took camels, and set to roam, To Mesopotamia, Nahor's town, his home.
By evening he stopped, where women drew water clear, Prayed for success, "Lord, let kindness appear.
Let the woman who offers camels a drink be the one, For Isaac, my master's beloved son."
Before he finished praying, Rebekah appeared, With her pitcher on her shoulder, she drew near.
Beautiful and pure, she went to the spring, He ran to meet her, with hope to bring.
"Please give me a little water," he asked with grace, She lowered her pitcher, a smile on her face.
"Drink, my lord," she said with care, "I'll draw for your camels, make sure they're fair."
He watched her in silence, till all was done, God had shown him, this was the one.
He gave her gold, asked, "Whose daughter are you?" She replied, "Bethuel's, plenty room for you, too."
The servant praised Yahweh, who guided his quest, To find a bride from Abraham's own nest.
Rebekah's brother, Laban, saw the treasures and heard, Invited the servant, "Welcome, spoken word."
Servant spoke of Abraham's wealth and God's plan, How he'd sworn to find Isaac's woman, not from Canaan.
Rebekah's family agreed, "It's God's will, we see, Take her, let her be Isaac's, let it be."
The servant bowed low, thanking the Lord, Gave gifts aplenty, his heart soared.
Rebekah's kin blessed her, with wishes so grand, She left on camels, holding destiny's hand.
Isaac was out in the field, deep in thought, Saw the camels, knew what they brought.
Rebekah veiled herself, asked, "Who is this man?" "It's my master," the servant said, as planned.
Isaac took Rebekah, into Sarah's tent, She became his wife, love's true testament.
Isaac found comfort, with Rebekah there, A love story written, beyond compare.
Abraham took a wife, Keturah's her name, Bore him Zimran, Jokshan, and a bustling fame. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan too, Midian had sons, a crew to pursue.
To Isaac, Abraham gave all his share, Sent the others east, with gifts to spare. Lived a full life, a hundred seventy-five, Gave up his spirit, no longer alive.
Isaac and Ishmael, buried him deep, In Machpelah's cave, where ancestors sleep. Field of Ephron, bought fair and square, With his wife Sarah, Abraham rests there.
Isaac's blessed, by God's own decree, Lived by Beer Lahai Roi, peacefully. Ishmael's history carried on, Hagar's son, from dusk till dawn.
Named his sons from Nebaioth to Kedemah, Twelve princes in villages, spreading afar. Ishmael lived full, one hundred thirty-seven, Passed from the earth, gathered in heaven.
Isaac's story unfolds, Abraham's line, Rebekah's his bride, fate intertwined. Prayed to God, her womb was barren, God heard, blessed with life, his love and caring.
Two nations in her womb, a heavenly test, "One will be stronger; the elder will serve the rest." Twins were born, Esau came first, Red and hairy, for greatness, a thirst.
Jacob followed, gripping the heel, Isaac was sixty, when twins were revealed. Esau, a hunter, loved by Dad, Jacob, tent dweller, made Mom glad.
Esau came hungry, from fields afar, Saw Jacob's stew, "Feed me, I'm scarred!" "First, your birthright," Jacob did say, Esau, famished, gave it away.
Sworn and sold, for bread and stew, Esau ate, despised what he knew. Rise and fall, a tale of strife, In birthright sold, Esau's life.
Famine in the land, same as before, Isaac heads to Gerar, seeking more. God appears, says, "Stay, don’t go south, In this land, I’ll bless you, word of mouth.
Your offspring’s stars will light up the sky, Through them, every nation will rise high. 'Cause Abraham listened to what I said, My laws, my voice, he always led."
Isaac in Gerar, playing it sly, "She’s my sister," was the cautious lie. Feared for his life, Rebekah’s beauty bright, Thought the men might kill, take her in the night.
Abimelech peeped from his window tall, Spotted Isaac and Rebekah, not sister at all. Called him out, "Why lie to us here? Could've brought guilt, made us live in fear!"
Abimelech warns, "Touch them you’ll be dead," God’s blessings fell, and Isaac was fed. Sowed and reaped, land gave its yield, Wealth grew large, blessings unsealed.
Philistines filled wells with earth and stone, Jealous of the riches Isaac owned. Abimelech said, "You’re too strong, go away," Isaac moved and settled, no delay.
Dug the wells, his father’s days renewed, Water springing forth, blessings pursued. Esek, Sitnah were wells they fought, Rehoboth came, space they sought.
God said, "Fear not, I’m with you still, For Abraham’s sake, blessings will fill." Built an altar, called Yahweh’s name, Isaac’s faith unshaken, ever the same.
Abimelech came to make things right, "We see God’s with you, no need to fight. Let’s make a pact, no harm, just peace, With Yahweh’s blessing, may we increase."
Feast was shared, oaths were sworn, Peaceful was the day, a new morn. Servants dug a well, water found, Called it Shibah, blessings abound.
Esau’s choices, Judith and Basemath, Brought grief to Isaac, a heavy path. But Isaac stood firm, blessings were near, With God’s promise, he had no fear.
Isaac was old, his eyes couldn't see, Called Esau, "My son?" "Here I am," said he.
"I'm old now, don't know when I'll die, Grab your bow, hunt some venison, make it by and by."
"Cook it up tasty, bring it to me, So my soul can bless you, let it be free."
Rebekah was listening, she heard it all, Esau went hunting, obeying the call.
Rebekah to Jacob whispers the plan, "Your dad's ready to bless Esau, understand?"
"Get two goats, I'll cook them just right, Your father will bless you, in disguise you'll take flight."
"But Esau's hairy, I'm smooth, what if he sees?" "Let the curse be on me, just do as I please."
So Jacob fetched the goats, brought them back home, His mother prepared them, like Isaac's own.
She dressed Jacob in Esau's best clothes, Put goat skins on his hands, on his neck they rose.
He brought the dish to Isaac, said "I'm your son." Isaac asked, "Who?" "Esau," said the one.
"How so quick?" Isaac questioned, surprised. "God gave me success," Jacob replied.
"Come closer, let me feel your hand," Isaac felt the hair, "Seems like Esau, grand."
He didn't recognize, so the blessing came, Asked again, "Are you Esau?" Jacob claimed the name.
Isaac ate the meal, enjoyed the wine, Blessed Jacob, "May nations serve, all align."
"Fruits of the earth, skies' morning dew, Be master over kin, may curses fall on who curses you."
Jacob just left as Esau walked in, With his own dish for the blessing to begin.
"Who are you?" Isaac asked, his heart missed a beat, "I'm your firstborn, Esau," came the repeat.
Isaac trembled, "Who got the blessing instead? I've blessed him already, your brother," he said.
Esau cried out, "Father, bless me too!" "Your brother deceived me, the blessing's through."
Esau lamented, "Twice he took my right, First my birthright, now my blessing, my plight."
Isaac replied, "Made him your lord, can't change, I've given grain and wine, it's been arranged."
Esau pleaded, "One blessing left for me?" Isaac spoke again, "Here's what yours will be."
"Live by the sword, serve your brother, But when you break free, you won't be smothered."
Esau burned with a grudge, plotted in mind, "After Dad's days, Jacob's fate I'll find."
Rebekah warned Jacob, "Your life's in danger here, Flee to Uncle Laban, till Esau's wrath is clear."
"Stay a while, let his anger subside, I'll call you back, when peace does abide."
She spoke to Isaac, weary of her life, "If Jacob marries Heth's daughter, it'll bring me strife."
Isaac called Jacob, blessed him with a plan, "Don't take a Canaanite woman, find your clan.
Rise and go to Paddan Aram, to Bethuel's place, From Laban's daughters, choose a wife with grace.
May God bless you, make you a nation so grand, Give you Abraham’s blessing, inherit the land."
Off Jacob went, journey set for Laban's gate, Esau saw the blessing, began to contemplate.
He noticed Jacob obeyed, followed the call, And realized the Canaan wives didn’t please at all.
So Esau turned to Ishmael, and took a new bride, Mahalath, his cousin, right by his side.
Jacob left Beersheba, headed towards Haran, Stopped as the sun set, laid his head on a stone, man.
He dreamed of a ladder, reaching high to the skies, Angels moving up and down, to his surprise.
Yahweh stood above, speaking clear and profound, "I’m God of your fathers, on this land you’re bound.
Your kin will spread wide, like dust on the earth, Through you every family will find their worth.
I’m with you always, won't leave you alone, Until every promise and blessing is known."
Jacob woke up, his heart filled with awe, "This place is God’s house, the gate to all law."
He took the stone, set it up high, Anointed it with oil, as the night passed by.
Called the place Bethel, where dreams were made, Vowed to God, if He’d guide him in the path he laid.
"If God stays with me, gives me food and attire, Brings me home in peace, as I desire.
Then this pillar will be God's house, no doubt, And a tenth of all blessings, I'll give as my shout."
Jacob traveled far, to the east he came, Saw a well and sheep, and learned their name.
Big stone on the well, heavy to move, Flocks gathered round, waiting in a groove.
"Where you from?" Jacob asked with care, "We're from Haran," they replied, standing there.
"Know Laban?" Jacob asked, eager to meet, "We know him well," their answer complete.
"Is it well?" Jacob asked with a smile, "Yes, Rachel comes," they said, "wait a while."
Sun high in the sky, Jacob said, "Water the sheep, then onward be led."
"We can’t," they replied, "till all gather round, Stone needs rolling, then water abounds."
Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, Jacob saw her, his heart took a leap.
He moved the stone, with strength and grace, Watered the flock, looked at Rachel's face.
He kissed her, wept, and spoke with pride, "I'm kin to your father," he proudly cried.
Rachel ran to tell her dad the news, Laban came running, no time to lose.
Laban embraced him, said, "You're my own," Jacob stayed, felt right at home.
"You’ll work," Laban said, "but what's your fee?" "Seven years for Rachel, let that be."
Laban agreed, "Better you than another, Stay with us, you’re like no other."
Seven years flew by like a dream, Jacob's love for Rachel, a steady stream.
"Give me my wife," Jacob said with a cheer, Laban prepared a feast, all were near.
But in the night, Leah was there, Jacob awoke, caught unaware.
"Why deceive me?" Jacob demanded, Laban's custom, not as he planned it.
"One more week, then Rachel's yours too, Seven more years, you know what to do."
Jacob agreed, worked seven more, Loved Rachel deeply, to his core.
Leah bore sons, Reuben was first, "Yahweh saw my pain, quenched my thirst."
Simeon came next, "Yahweh heard my cries," Levi followed, hope in her eyes.
Judah was born, "I'll praise Yahweh," Then Leah's bearing ceased that day.
Rachel cried to Jacob, feeling cold and bare, "Give me children, or else I can't bear!"
Jacob fired back, his patience worn thin, "Am I like God, who keeps life within?"
Rachel had a plan, with a voice so sly, "Take Bilhah, my maid, let her give it a try."
Jacob did as she said, Bilhah conceived and bore, Rachel named him Dan, her faith restored.
Again Bilhah bore, another son to claim, Rachel said, "I've won," Naphtali was his name.
Leah saw her time had ceased, and gave Zilpah to wed, Zilpah bore a son, and Leah laughed, "Gad, what a spread!"
Once more Zilpah bore, and Asher's name did she declare, "Happy am I, they'll call me blessed everywhere."
Reuben found some mandrakes ripe in the field, Rachel wanted them, her need revealed.
Leah struck a deal, with a mandrake’s worth, "You can have him tonight," for Rachel's mirth.
Leah bore Jacob yet another son so bright, "Issachar," she said, "God's given me my right."
Then came Zebulun, Leah's sixth child, "Now my husband's heart is reconciled."
And later, Dinah, a daughter gracing her line, Rachel prayed for her chance, her own son to shine.
God remembered Rachel, her womb opened wide, She bore Joseph, joy she couldn't hide.
Jacob said to Laban, "Let me take my leave, I’ve served you well, my own family I must retrieve."
Laban wanted him to stay, for blessings he knew, "Just name your price, I'll make it come true."
Jacob planned with wisdom, sheep and goats as his hire, "I'll take the speckled and spotted, that's my desire."
Laban agreed, but slyly set a snare, Stripped the marked ones, leaving Jacob to fare.
Three days apart, Jacob's plan took root, Rods peeled and placed, the strong ones bore fruit.
He separated the flocks, the stronger became his, Feeble stayed Laban’s, Jacob rising in bliss.
His wealth grew vast, flocks and servants galore, Camels and donkeys, a prosperous score.

Jacob heard the whispers, Laban's sons complain, "He's taken all our father's wealth, left us nothing to gain." He saw Laban's face, not friendly as before, Yahweh said, "Return home, I'll guide you and more."

Called Rachel and Leah to the field, Jacob shared, "Your father's not the same, but God's been there, prepared. I've served with strength, though he deceived me ten times, But God didn't let him hurt me; justice in his rhymes."
"If speckled, they're mine, if streaked, they bear the name, God took his livestock, handed me the acclaim. In a dream, I saw goats marked and leaped, The angel spoke, 'I'm the God you vowed to keep.
Now rise, leave this land, return to your birth's plan.'" Rachel and Leah said, "We have no place in this man. What God gave us is ours, it's clear as you see, Now do what God told you, let it be."
Jacob packed up, set his camels on the track, Took all his goods, not looking back. While Laban sheared sheep, Rachel took his teraphim sly, Jacob left without a word, under the night sky.
On the third day, Laban learned Jacob fled, He gathered his kin, chased with anger and dread. In a dream, God warned Laban, "Speak no good or bad," Laban caught up, frustrated and mad.
"What have you done? Why sneak away, deceive? I would've sent you off with music, or so I believe. But God said beware, so here I stand, Yet, why take my gods from my hand?"
Jacob replied, "I feared you'd strip me bare, But search my camp, find them if you dare." Laban searched tents, but Rachel was shrewd, She hid the teraphim, her father she eluded.
"Forgive me, I can't rise, it's a woman's time," Laban searched in vain, missed the hidden crime. Jacob's anger sparked, "What sin have I made? You've searched my things, found nothing to trade."
"Twenty years I served, never a lamb I ate, Bore the loss myself, endured day and night without fate. Fourteen years for daughters, six years for flocks, God saw my toil, and struck the clocks."
Laban said, "All you have is mine to see, But let's make a covenant, just you and me." Jacob raised a stone, set it as a sign, Laban and he agreed, "This stone marks the line."
A witness heap, and Mizpah, a watchful decree, "Yahweh sees us both, here and when we're free." A warning not to harm, cross the line with ill, They swore by their fathers, sealing God's will.
Jacob's sacrifice, a meal shared on the hill, Laban blessed his kin, then departed, the scene still. Early morning farewell, with kisses and grace, Laban departed, returned to his place.
Jacob on his journey, angels in his sight, "This is God's army," he knew it was right.
To Esau, his brother, messengers he sent, To the land of Seir, his words were meant.
"Tell Esau, your servant Jacob speaks, With Laban I've lived, so now I seek."
"I've got cattle, donkeys, flocks in line, Please show me favor, let your face shine."
Messengers returned, with news they bring, "Esau's coming with four hundred, like a king."
Jacob felt fear, his heart it raced, Divided his people, each group in its place.
"If Esau strikes one, the other will flee, A chance to escape, safety for me."
He prayed, "God of my fathers, hear my plea, You promised good, now deliver me."
From Esau's hand, protect me now, I fear his wrath, before him I bow.
"You promised my offspring, like the sea's sand, Too many to count, by Your guiding hand."
That night he stayed, gifts he prepared, Goats, rams, camels, all carefully shared.
To his servants he said, "Go ahead in line, Tell Esau, Jacob's gift, a peace sign."
He ordered them all, the same to declare, "Jacob comes behind, his gifts to share."
The gift went ahead, while Jacob stayed, Night came, he crossed Jabbok, unafraid.
Alone he wrestled, 'til dawn did break, The man touched his thigh, made him ache.
"Let me go," the man said with the light, "Not unless you bless me," Jacob held tight.
"What's your name?" the man did inquire, "Jacob," he answered, heart full of fire.
"No more Jacob, Israel you'll be, You've wrestled with God, and found victory."
"Tell me your name," Jacob asked, "Why ask?" the man said, in blessing he basked.
Jacob named it Peniel, face to face he'd met, God preserved his life, he'd never forget.
As the sun rose, he limped on his way, A reminder of the struggle, to this very day.
The children of Israel keep the tale alive, The sinew of the hip, a legacy to survive.
Jacob looked up, saw Esau drawing near, With four hundred men, a sight to fear. He split the kids between Leah, Rachel, and crew, Servants first, then Leah, Rachel and Joseph in view.
He walked ahead, bowed seven times on the ground, Till near his brother, no fear to be found. Esau ran, embraced, necks entwined, Kissed him, and both hearts aligned.
Esau looked, saw the women and kids, "Who are these?" Jacob said, "Gifts from God, given with ease." Servants came near, bowing low, Leah and kids followed, moving slow.
Esau asked, "Why all this crew?" Jacob replied, "To find favor with you." Esau said, "Brother, enough I own, Let what you have remain your own."
Jacob pleaded, "If I've found favor, take this from me, I've seen your face, like God’s it be." "God’s been gracious, I have my share," Esau accepted, a bond so rare.
Esau said, "Let’s journey, I'll lead the way," Jacob responded, "Pace is key for today. Kids are tender, flocks are young, We’ll move gently, till the journey's done."
Esau offered help, Jacob declined, "Find favor in your sight, in peace I'm aligned." Esau returned to Seir, his own route clear, While Jacob to Succoth, shelters to rear.
In Shechem's land, peace was found, Bought land from Hamor, tent on the ground. Built an altar, strong and real, Called it El Elohe Israel.
Dinah stepped out to see the land, Shechem saw her, took her hand. He laid with her, brought her low, Yet love for Dinah in him did grow.
To his father, Shechem made his plea, "Get her for my wife, she’s meant for me." Jacob heard the cries but kept his peace, His sons in the field, no release.
Hamor came to Jacob’s place, The sons returned, anger on their face. “This wrong done to our kin!” they cried, A tale of disgrace they couldn't abide.
Hamor pleaded, "Please comply, Let my son wed, don't deny. Join with us, be one kin, Trade and prosper, let's begin."
Shechem vowed, “Tell me the price, I'll pay in full, no sacrifice, Just give Dinah as my bride, I'll meet your terms, I won't hide.”
But Jacob’s sons with deceit replied, “We can’t give sister to your uncircumcised. Do as we do, that’s our play, Then we’ll join you, without delay.”
Hamor and Shechem liked the plan, To the city gate, they spoke to every man. “Let’s join with them, it’ll be grand, Their wealth will be ours, like we planned.”
Every male did heed the call, Circumcised, one and all. On the third day, in pain and strife, Simeon and Levi took to life.
With swords they came, swift and keen, Hamor and Shechem, no more seen. They took Dinah, left the town, Jacob's sons brought the city down.
Plundered riches, took their kin, Retaliation for the sin.
Jacob scolded, "What have you done? I’m outnumbered, we can't outrun!" The brothers stood, defiant gleam, “Should he treat her like a dream?”
"Jacob, arise, head to Bethel's land, Make an altar there, as I command."
To his household, Jacob did declare, "Rid yourselves of gods and clothes, make yourselves bare. We'll rise and head to Bethel's holy space, Where God answered me in my distressful chase."
They handed him their idols, without delay, Jacob hid them beneath an oak by Shechem's way. As they traveled on, fear struck the towns around, They left Jacob's sons alone, no enemies were found.
Jacob reached Luz, now Bethel in Canaan's land, With his people, he did stand. Built an altar there, called it El Beth El, For God had revealed Himself when Jacob fell.
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, met her fate, Buried below Bethel, by the oak's gate. God appeared to Jacob, once again, Blessed him with a name change, breaking the chain.
"No more Jacob, Israel's your name, A nation you'll become, kings will proclaim. The land I promised to Abraham and Isaac, it’s yours, To your offspring, this land endures."
God departed, left His mark in the place, Jacob set a stone, an altar of grace. Poured oil and drink, Bethel’s name he sealed, Then onward they traveled, destinies revealed.
Rachel labored hard on the road to Ephrath, A son was born, her life's final path. "Don't fear," said the midwife, "a son's here, Benoni she named him, Benjamin, his father held dear."
