He camped on Hachilah's hill, by desert's side, David watched from afar, knew he couldn't hide.
Sent out his spies, learned Saul was near, Gathered his courage, banished his fear.
David asked Ahimelech, Abishai, his crew, "Who'll go with me to where Saul's army grew?"
Abishai stepped up, "Brother, I'll stand, With you at night in Saul's encamped land."
So, by night, they crept, where Saul lay still, Spear by his head, sleeping, no ill will.
Abishai whispered, "God delivered him here, Let me pin him down with one thrust, no fear."
But David said, "No harm to God's chosen, Can't strike the anointed, leave him unbroken."
"As the Lord lives, He’ll decide Saul's fate, But don't raise your hand, let’s just take."
Took the spear, the jar, from near Saul's head, Tiptoed away while God's deep sleep spread.
From the mountain afar, David then cried, Called out to Abner, with anger, he chided:
"Aren't you meant to guard the king's life? Someone snuck in, could’ve ended the strife!"
“Look for the spear and the jar, now gone, You’ve failed your duty, the threat was strong.”
Saul heard the voice, "Is that you, my son?" David replied, "It's me, O king, what have I done?"
"Why chase me down, what wrong have I set? If God sent you, let’s make amends yet."
"But if men cursed me, drove me away, Don’t spill my blood, near Yahweh I’ll stay."
Saul acknowledged, "I've sinned, my son, Come back, I won’t harm, this chase is done."
David called back, "Here’s the spear, proof in my hand, Let your men fetch it, on righteousness we stand."
"May God reward as He sees fit, I spared your life, and that’s legit."
Saul responded, "Bless you, my son, You’ll do great things, your battles well won."
David turned, went his own way, While Saul, in his place, chose to stay.
David thought in his heart, "One day, Saul's hand Will end me, so I'll flee to Philistine land. With Saul in despair, searching no more, I'll escape his grasp, be free, for sure."
So David arose, with six hundred bold, To Gath's king Achish, like a story told. With his wives and men, he settled there, In Achish's land, without a care.
Saul heard the news, David had fled, He stopped his pursuit, thought David was dead. David to Achish made a plea, "Let me live in a town, away from royalty."
Achish gave him Ziklag, a place to reside, Ziklag, a gift now, in Judah's pride. For a year and four months, David stayed, Raiding the lands, in the Philistine shade.
Geshurites, Girzites, Amalekites too, David struck them down, none were left to view. Sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels he'd take, No man or woman left for truth to break.
Back to Achish, who asked, "Whom did you fight?" "South of Judah, Jerahmeelites, Kenites," was his light. No captives alive, to Gath he brought, "None to tell tales, none to report."
Achish believed him, said with glee, "Israel hates him, he'll serve only me."
Philistines gathered, armies in the fray, Achish told David, "You'll fight with me today." David replied, "You'll see what I can do," Achish said, "Bodyguard, forever, that's you."
Now Samuel's gone, all Israel mourned deep, Buried in Ramah, where he'd forever sleep. Saul sent away spirits, wizards too, Philistines camped in Shunem, with a view.
Saul saw the foe, his heart trembled with fear, He called to Yahweh, but no answer was near. "Find me a woman, a spirit she'll bring," "There's one in Endor," was their offering.
Saul in disguise, with two men in the night, To the woman he said, "Bring a spirit to light." The woman replied, "Saul's cut us out," "Why lay a snare, put my life in doubt?"
Saul swore, "No harm will come by Yahweh's breath," "Who'll I bring?" "Bring Samuel from death." She saw Samuel, cried out in fright, "Why deceive me? You're Saul in the night!"
"Don't be scared," Saul assured, "What do you see?" "A god from the earth, coming to me." "Describe him," Saul asked, "What's his attire?" "An old man, robed," she spoke of the sire.
Saul knew it was Samuel, bowed low, Samuel said, "Why disturb me so?" Saul answered, "I'm distressed, foes at my gate, God's gone, no word, tell me my fate."
"Why ask me?" Samuel's voice thundered loud, "Yahweh's left you, and no longer proud. The kingdom's torn, given to David's hand, For disobeying Yahweh's command.
Philistines shall seize, you and sons won't be, With me tomorrow, in death you'll greet me." Saul fell flat, terrified by the news, Weak from hunger, lost and confused.
The woman saw Saul, troubled and frail, "Listen to me, let me end this tale. Eat for strength, go on your way," He refused but they urged him to stay.
With a calf she cooked, bread made quick, Saul and his men ate, feeling sick. Then they rose, went away into the night, Heavy with the words, and their future's plight.
Philistines gathered, armies at Aphek's gate, Israelites by Jezreel, they await their fate.
Philistine lords pass in ranks, all in line, David with Achish, in the rear, biding time.
Princes see David, they ask, "Who are these guys?" Achish replies, "It's David, no surprise.
He's been with me for years, no fault in him found, He left Saul's side, stuck with me, battle-bound."
Princes are angry, "Send him back home, Don’t want him with us, let him roam.
In the fight, what if he turns on us all? Could he win back Saul with our heads as his haul?
Isn't this David of the songs they sing, ‘Saul slayed thousands, David ten thousand he'd bring?’”
Achish calls David, says, "By Yahweh you’re true, Your comings and goings, they’re good in my view.
But lords aren't pleased, so don't take offense, Return in peace, it makes the most sense."
David protests, "What wrong have I done? I've stood by you, faithful as the sun.
Why can't I fight with you, against your foes?" Achish responds, "I know how this goes.
You're like an angel, bright in my sight, But princes say no, they won't let you fight.
Rise up early, take your men, and go, At morning's light, depart soft and slow."
David rose early, his men by his side, Back to Philistine land, they did glide.
Philistines marched on, to Jezreel they pressed, The battle awaited, with tension and unrest.
David and his crew came back to Ziklag on the third, Only to find it burned, a sight so absurd. The Amalekites raided, took the young and the old, Left the place in ashes, their plan so bold.
No lives were lost, but captives they did take, David's heart sank, for his wives were at stake. The men cried out, their sorrow so deep, Until they had no more tears left to weep.
In distress and fear, whispers of blame, They talked of stoning him, speaking his name. But David turned to God, heart full of might, Strengthened by Yahweh, ready to fight.

He called for Abiathar, "Bring the ephod here," And sought the Lord's guidance, his path to clear. "Should I chase them down? Will I win this race?" "Pursue them," God said, "you’ll reclaim your place."
So David set out with six hundred strong, But two hundred were faint, couldn't go along. With four hundred left, they crossed the brook, In search of their families, every corner they'd look.
Found an Egyptian, weak in the field, Fed him well, his secrets revealed. "I was left for sick, a servant's fate, We raided Ziklag, now I narrate."
"Can you lead us there?" David did inquire, "Swear you won't kill me," was his lone desire. The Egyptian agreed, led David right down, To find the raiders spread all around.
Feasting and dancing on the spoils they had, David struck them down, his wrath was mad. From twilight till evening, he fought with skill, Except for four hundred who fled on camels, quick to spill.
David reclaimed all, not a thing was missed, His wives, the young, their plundered list. "This is David's bounty," the people said, As they returned with flocks, well fed.
To the ones who stayed behind, David shared, "We split this evenly, as Yahweh cared." "From this day forward, let it be known, In battle or baggage, the share's our own."
David sent gifts, shared the joy and the gain, To Judah's elders, they received his reign. To Bethel, Ramoth, and places of old, To all who supported, their friendship bold.
Philistines on the rise, Israel in retreat, Mount Gilboa where they faced defeat. Saul's sons they fell, Jonathan too, Philistines took them, nothing they could do.
Arrows flew, Saul was distressed, He called to his bearer, "End this, bring me rest." But fear gripped him, the task he declined, So Saul took his sword, a tragic end defined.
His armor bearer followed, loyal to the core, Saul and sons gone, their story no more. Israel saw, fled cities, left behind, Philistines moved in, new homes to find.
Next day the victors came, to strip the dead, Saw Saul's broken body, took his head. Armor displayed in Ashtaroth's shrine, Body on Beth Shan, a dark design.
Jabesh Gilead heard of Saul's fate, Valiant men rose, never too late. Through the night they marched, on a rescue quest, Took bodies home, laid them to rest.
Bones buried under tamarisk's shade, Seven days they fasted, farewell made.
After Saul's demise, David's back in the zone, From fighting Amalekites, Ziklag his home. Then on the third day, a man appeared, Clothes all torn, with dust upon his beard.
He dropped to the ground, respect he showed, David asked, "From where's your road?" "I escaped the camp of Israel's fight," The man replied, "from battle's night."
David pressed, "What's the battle's tale?" "The people fled, the brave did fail. Saul and Jonathan, they're laid to rest." David's heart sunk, his spirit compressed.
"How do you know?" David needed to see, "On Mount Gilboa, Saul called to me. Leaning on his spear, chariots in chase, I heard my name and saw his face."
"Who are you?" Saul did inquire, "An Amalekite," I did declare. "Stand by and take my life, Anguish grips me, end this strife."
I did his bidding, took crown and band, Brought them here, as you command." David tore his clothes, his men did the same, Weeping, fasting, for the fallen's name.
"Why no fear to harm Yahweh’s choice?" David questioned with a steady voice. "Strike him down," David did decide, For the truth his own lips supplied.
David mourned, "Your glory slain, How the mighty have fallen, their strength in vain. Don’t spread it in Gath, let Ashkelon remain still, Lest their daughters rejoice on each hill."
Mountains of Gilboa, no rain should fall, For there the shields were cast withal. Jonathan's bow stayed true, Saul's sword never failed, In life and death, their unity prevailed.
Daughters of Israel, mourn in your scarlet thread, For Saul who clothed and adorned you has fled. How the mighty fell in battle's heat, Jonathan’s death, a bitter defeat.
My brother Jonathan, distress I find, Your love was beyond, to my heart aligned. How the mighty have fallen, their weapons at rest, The heroes lie silent, in their eternal quest.
David asked the Lord, "Should I head to Judah's land?" God replied, "Yes, go up as planned."
"Where to?" David asked, seeking the zone. God said, "To Hebron, make it your throne."
David packed up with his wives by his side, Ahinoam and Abigail, off for the ride.
His men came too, each with his kin, They settled in Hebron, their new life to begin.
Judah's men came, crowned David their king, They spoke of Saul's burial, a noble thing.
David sent word to Jabesh Gilead, blessed them so, "Yahweh's kindness and truth, may you know.
For this great act, I reward your grace, Be strong, be brave, in this new place."
Meanwhile, Abner brought Ishbosheth to reign, Over tribes of Israel, a kingdom to gain.
But Judah held firm, David was their choice, Seven years and six months, they raised their voice.
Abner and Joab by Gibeon's pool, Two armies sat, tensions cool.
"Let young men duel," Abner did suggest, "Let them arise," Joab agreed to the test.
Twelve from each side took the stand, Swords clashed, fell together, blood stained the land.
Battle raged on, fierce was the day, David's servants drove Abner away.
Asahel ran swift, like a gazelle on the chase, Abner turned, saw him, "Is that you?" he faced.
"Turn aside," Abner urged, but Asahel pressed, "Why must I harm you, give Joab no rest?"
But Asahel refused, so Abner struck hard, The spear went through, Asahel lay scarred.
Joab and Abishai chased through the night, Abner called, "End this endless fight!"
Joab replied, "Had you not spoken, The dawn would see no brother broken."
The trumpet was blown, the fighting ceased, Each side retreated, seeking peace.
Abner crossed Jordan, back to his camp, Joab paused, counted, nineteen fell in the stamp.
Three hundred sixty of Abner's men lay, Asahel was buried at Bethlehem next day.
Joab's men marched through the night, Back to Hebron, with dawn's first light.
In Hebron, David’s house grew strong and bold, While Saul’s house weakened, its story told.
David had sons, born one by one, Amnon, Chileab, Absalom, their life begun.
Adonijah, Shephatiah, Ithream too, In Hebron these sons of David grew.
Abner gained power, Saul’s house on his side, But Ishbosheth’s words made his anger rise wide.
“Am I a dog’s head with Judah’s crew? I’ve kept you safe, yet you question what I do!”
“God do more if I don't keep David’s throne, From Saul’s house, to rule from land to known.”
Abner sent word, “Let’s make this deal, Bring all Israel, for David’s appeal.”
David replied, “Make this treaty be, But bring Michal, and you’ll see me.”
Ishbosheth sent for her, took her away, Paltiel wept, but to Bahurim he’d stay.
Abner spoke to Israel, “David’s your king, Yahweh’s promise, salvation he’ll bring.”
Abner came to David with twenty men, And David feasted, peace reigned again.
Joab returned from a raid with his band, He learned Abner came, but left the land.
“What have you done?” Joab asked the king, “Abner’s deceit, he knows everything.”
Joab called Abner back, at the gate he did meet, Struck him down, for his brother's defeat.
David mourned, “I’m guiltless of this blood, Let Joab’s house bear the flood.”
“Clothe in sackcloth, mourn Abner this day,” David followed the bier, leading the way.
“Should Abner fall like a fool in the dust, With no bonds or chains, betrayed by unjust?”
David wept, the people joined the cry, He swore not to eat till the sun passed by.
The people saw and it pleased them right, The king’s heart was clear in their sight.
“A great man’s fallen, though I’m weak today, May Yahweh judge the wicked, for their wicked way.”
Saul's son heard of Abner's fall, His hands grew weak, his spirit small. Israel trembled, stricken with fear, Two raider captains were drawing near.
Baanah and Rechab, brothers in crime, From Beeroth's land, Benjamin's line. Jonathan's boy, young but lame, Mephibosheth was his name.
Rechab and Baanah, in the heat of the day, To Ishbosheth's house, they made their way. Pretended to fetch wheat, all was still, Struck him down as he lay in the chill.
In his bed, they took his breath, Killed and beheaded, sealing his death. They seized his head, off to David they sped, Through the night, in the Arabah, they tread.
To Hebron with Ishbosheth's head they came, "Here's Saul's son's head," they proclaimed. "Yahweh avenged you, King, this day, Saul's end is here," they dared to say.
David replied with a heart full of fire, “As Yahweh lives, my soul's true supplier, When news of Saul's death came to me, I rewarded the bearer with fatal decree.
Now you wicked men, who killed a just soul, In his own bed, you've paid the toll." David commanded, justice was set, Hands and feet cut, a grim silhouette.
Beside Hebron's pool, their fate was sealed, Ishbosheth's head, in Abner's field. David made sure it all was done, Justice served, the light of the sun.
All the tribes gathered, their voices were strong, "We're your bone and flesh, we've been here all along.
Back when Saul reigned, you led us in and out, Yahweh said, 'You'll lead, of that there's no doubt.'
Elders came to Hebron, in front of Yahweh they stood, With a covenant made, David's rule was understood.
Thirty years young, he began his reign, Forty years on, his leadership plain.
Seven years and some months he ruled in Hebron's sight, Then thirty-three in Jerusalem, his kingdom bright.
To Jerusalem he marched, the Jebusites defiant, "The blind and lame will stop you," they were reliant.
Yet David took Zion, now called David's town, "Strike the blind and lame," he said, taking them down.
In his stronghold he lived, his city named, David built around, his greatness proclaimed.
With Yahweh on his side, David rose higher, Hiram of Tyre sent gifts to inspire.
Cedar, carpenters, and masons came along, A house for David, where he would belong.
He knew Yahweh's hand established him king, For Israel's sake, the praises they'd sing.
More concubines and wives, his family grew wide, Sons and daughters born, his legacy applied.
Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon fair, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia there.
Elishama, Eliada, Eliphelet named, In Jerusalem, their heritage claimed.
Philistines heard of David, anointed and true, They sought him out, but he knew what to do.
Down to the stronghold David did go, The Philistines spread out, their numbers did grow.
"Shall I fight them, Yahweh?" David inquired, "Go up," said Yahweh, "their defeat is desired."
Baal Perazim, the battle was won, "Yahweh broke them like waters," David's shout was done.
They left their idols, to David's men they stayed, Philistines returned, but Yahweh's plan was laid.
"Circle behind, wait by the mulberry trees, When you hear them march, move with ease."
Yahweh led the charge, Philistines fell, From Geba to Gezer, David's story to tell.
David gathered thirty thousand, a chosen mighty band, To bring God's ark from Judah's land, a task so grand.
They set the ark on a cart, new and bright, Uzzah and Ahio drove it, guiding it right.
Instruments played, cypress wood, harps in hand, Tambourines, cymbals—music filled the land.
But at Nacon's floor, Uzzah reached out bold, The cattle stumbled, the ark's touch was cold.
God's anger burned, Uzzah fell, struck down, David, displeased, named the place with a frown.
"How can Yahweh's ark come to me?" David cried, Afraid, he left it, in Obed-Edom's house to abide.
For three months it stayed, blessings poured down, David heard the news, joy spread around the town.
He went to bring the ark, joyfully to his city, Six paces in, they sacrificed with heartfelt pity.
David danced with might, in linen ephod he spun, Shouting, trumpets blared, a celebration begun.
Michal watched from the window, despising the scene, As David danced before Yahweh, heart open and keen.
The ark found its place in a tent set with care, Burnt offerings, peace offerings, David's prayer.
To all the people, bread, dates, raisins as a feast, A blessing in Yahweh's name, joy increased.
Michal scorned, "How glorious today, your display!" But David replied, "Before Yahweh, I'd dance this way."
"I'll be more vile, in my own sight less, Yet the maids will honor me, my joy confess."
And Michal, childless, lived on through her days, As David danced on, giving Yahweh his praise.

The king sat at peace, his battles all done, Said to Nathan, "Look, I've got a house of cedar, son. But the Ark of God stays behind a curtain thin." Nathan said, "Do what's in your heart; Yahweh's with you within."
That night Yahweh spoke to Nathan clear, "Tell David, 'Should you build me a house here? I've roamed in tents since Egypt set them free, Did I ask for cedar walls surrounding me?
Remember David, where you came from, the sheep, I made you a prince, gave you enemies' defeat. I'll make your name great, like giants of old, Plant Israel firm, their story unfold.
I'll give them peace, their troubles will cease, And David, I'll build you a house in my lease. When your days are done, and you're laid to rest, Your offspring will rise, kingdom blessed.
He'll build for my name, his throne will last, I'll be his father, his future's cast. If he errs, he'll bear the human rod, Yet my love won't leave, unlike Saul's flawed.
Your house, your reign, forever secure, Your throne established, this promise is pure." Nathan told David every word, every sight, The king sat with Yahweh, in this divine light.
"Who am I, Lord Yahweh? What is my line? That you've brought me this far, in your grand design. This promise extends beyond what I see, You've chosen my house for eternity.
No words can express, for you know me well, Your greatness is clear, no story can tell. Israel redeemed, a people of your own, You made them a name, in lands they were shown.
Yahweh, confirm your word, let it be, Magnify your name, for all to see. You promised a house to stand evermore, Blessed be this house, forever in your lore."
David stepped up, struck the Philistine land, Took their city's power, wrested it from their hand.
He marched to Moab, with a line he measured, Two parts gone, one part kept, a decision he treasured.
Servants they became, tribute they brought, David's reign expanded, battles he fought.
Hadadezer of Zobah, next in line, David took his soldiers, claimed them as mine.
Seventeen hundred horsemen, twenty thousand on foot, Chariots hamstrung, a hundred he took.
Syrians of Damascus tried to lend aid, David struck twenty-two thousand, made them afraid.
Garrisons in Syria, they served him now, Tribute to David, Yahweh's gift, take a bow.
Golden shields from Hadadezer brought to town, Betah and Berothai's bronze made David renown.
Toi of Hamath, hearing of David's might, Sent his son Joram, with gifts shining bright.
Silver and gold, they arrived at his feet, David dedicated all to Yahweh, complete.
Nations he subdued, from Moab to Philistine, Ammon, Amalek, all he did oversee.
In the Valley of Salt, David's name became known, Eighteen thousand Syrians, his power was shown.
Edom secured, garrisons placed all around, The Edomites served, Yahweh's victory profound.
David ruled Israel with fairness and might, Justice and righteousness were his guiding light.
Joab, the commander, led with a strong hand, Jehoshaphat recorded the events of the land.
Zadok and Ahimelech were priests in the scene, Seraiah the scribe, keeping the records clean.
Benaiah over guards, the Cherethites and Pelethites, David’s sons as ministers, guiding people’s rights.
David wondered, "Is there anyone left from Saul's line? Jonathan's sake, I'm showing kindness, it's time to shine."
A servant named Ziba, from Saul's house, came near. "Are you Ziba?" the king asked. "Yes, I'm here."
"Is there anyone left from Saul's family, I pray? To show God's kindness, in a generous way?"
"Jonathan has a son," Ziba said, "though he's lame." "In Machir's house, Lo Debar, that's his name."
So King David sent for him, brought him from afar, From Machir's house, Lo Debar, under David's star.
Mephibosheth bowed low, respect on his face. David called, "Mephibosheth," in the king's place.
"Don't be afraid," David said, "kindness you'll see, For Jonathan's sake, your father's land, I decree.
At my table, you'll eat, bread without strife, Restored lands to you, a secure, honored life."
"What am I," he asked, "a dead dog you'd seek?" Yet David showed kindness to the humble and meek.
To Ziba, the king said, "All Saul had, it's done, For Mephibosheth, your master's son."
"Work the land, bring the harvest in hand, But Mephibosheth eats at my table, understand?"
Ziba agreed, with fifteen sons, twenty men, "All you command, I'll fulfill, again and again."
Mephibosheth dined, like a king's son, with pride, In Jerusalem, at the table, he'd abide.
His son Mica watched his father, glad to see, How kindness and grace from the king set him free.
Though lame in his feet, Mephibosheth's heart soared, For at David's table, he was always restored.

The king of Ammon passed, Hanun took his throne, David said, "I'll show kindness, the seed's been sown." Sent his servants to Hanun, in his grief to console, But Ammon's princes whispered, sowing doubt in the soul.

"Is David here to honor, or is it a spy game? Is he here to comfort or to claim Ammon's fame?" Hanun listened, took the servants, shaved half their beards, Cut their garments, sent them off in shame and fears.
Word reached David, he met them, saw their disgrace, "Stay in Jericho till your beards replace." Ammon saw they were foul in David's sight, Called Syrians for battle, gearing up for a fight.
David heard the news, sent Joab with the force, Ammon lined up at the gate in full course. Joab, seeing foes both front and back, Chose Israel's best, prepared for the attack.
"If Syrians press, then come lend me aid, If Ammon's too strong, I'll come with brigade. Be brave for our people, for the cities we hold, Let Yahweh decide what's good, what's bold."
Joab charged, Syrians fled from his sight, Ammon saw them run, took flight from the fight. Joab returned to the city, back home they trod, Syrians regrouped, plotting against the rod.
Hadadezer summoned forces, crossed the river wide, Shobach led with might, ready to collide. David gathered Israel, crossed Jordan's wide stream, Met Syrians in Helam, battle's brutal dream.
Syrians fled, David's strength held strong, Seven hundred charioteers, forty thousand gone. Struck down Shobach, their captain fell that day, Kings under Hadadezer saw defeat, turned away.
Peace they sought, with Israel they made, Syrians feared to help Ammon, with their aid they stayed.
In the springtime, when kings go to fight, David sent Joab, his army, a fearsome sight. They crushed Ammon and laid Rabbah under siege, But David stayed back, in Jerusalem’s peace.
One evening, restlessly he roamed his roof high, Saw a woman bathing, caught his eye. "Who is this beauty?" he asked with intent, "Bathsheba," they told him, "Uriah's wife, heaven-sent."
So David summoned her, and she came near, He knew her well, then she disappeared. Later she sent word, "I'm with child," David’s heart raced, his thoughts ran wild.
"Bring me Uriah," David decreed, Joab sent him back, fulfilling the need. David inquired of how Joab fared, "Go home, rest, let your worries be spared."
But loyal Uriah stayed by the gate, With servants he slept, his duty innate. David was puzzled, called him back too, "Why not go home, enjoy what’s due?"
"The ark, the troops, they’re in the fields," he pled, "I can’t enjoy comforts, while they shed." David persisted, "Stay one more day," Made Uriah drink, but firm he'd stay.
Next morning, David wrote with a heavy heart, Sent Uriah to Joab, played his part. "Put him upfront where the battle's hot, Then step back, leave him in that spot."
Joab obeyed, at the city’s edge, Uriah fell—war’s tragic pledge. News came to David, the report was grim, "Uriah's gone, others too, fallen victims."
David replied, "Let Joab press on, Strengthen the fight, until the city's gone." Bathsheba mourned, her tears were real, But soon joined David, a new life to feel.
Yet in this tale, God's displeasure reigned, David’s choices marked, consequences gained.

Nathan came to David, with a tale to unfold, About two men in a city, one rich, one with pockets cold. The rich man had flocks, more than he could ever need, The poor man just one lamb, his heart's only feed.
The lamb grew with him, like a daughter it stayed, A traveler came, and the rich man betrayed. He took the poor man's lamb, prepared it for the guest, David burned with anger, his fury didn't rest.
"As Yahweh lives," David shouted out, "The man who did this deserves to be knocked out. Restore the lamb four times, for this heartless act, No pity in his heart, that's a matter of fact."
Nathan pointed to David, "You are the man," he said, "Yahweh's words to you, listen and dread. I made you king, took you from Saul's hand, Gave you your master's house, and all the land."

"Yet you struck down Uriah, took his wife as your own, Evil in Yahweh's sight, now seeds of trouble are sown. The sword won’t leave your house, for the wrongs you've done, Your wives given to your neighbor, in the sight of the sun."
David confessed, "I have sinned against Yahweh's name," Nathan replied, "Your sin’s put away, but sorrow still came. The child shall die, for bringing shame to Yahweh's fame."

David mourned and fasted, pleading on the ground, But on the seventh day, silence was the sound. His servants feared the truth, their whispers caught his ear, "Is the child dead?" David asked, his voice sincere.

"He is dead," they replied, sorrow in their tone, David rose, washed, worshiped, on Yahweh’s throne. He ate and explained, "Who knows if grace would save, But now he’s gone, I shall join him in the grave."
Comforted Bathsheba, and they bore a son, Named Solomon, Yahweh's love to him was won. Nathan came again, and Jedidiah was his name, For Yahweh's sake, a child of great fame.
Meanwhile, Joab fought and Rabbah fell, He sent for David, with victories to tell. David gathered troops, took the city’s crown, Placed it on his head, wore Ammon’s renown.

From Ephraim to Jokmeam, names unfold, Ben Hur, Ben Deker, stories told. Ben Hesed, Ben Abinadab, held their ground, Baana, in Beth Shean, his duties renowned.
Ben Geber in Ramoth Gilead staked his claim, Ahinadab in Mahanaim held a similar aim. Ahimaaz took Solomon's daughter as wife, In Naphtali he lived a prosperous life.
Solomon’s rule stretched far and wide, From riverbanks to where the Philistines abide. Tribute flowed in, his kingdom secure, With wisdom and peace, his reign was pure.
Daily provisions—a feast arrayed, Cattle and sheep, in abundance displayed. Dominion stretched from Tiphsah to Gaza's reach, His wisdom like sand on the seashore's beach.
Forty thousand horses, chariots in rows, Twelve thousand riders, ready to go. Officers made sure the table stayed full, Barley and straw, the horses' pull.
God gave him wisdom, like none before, He spoke proverbs and songs, a thousand more. From cedars to hyssop, he knew them all, People came from nations to hear his call.
Solomon, wise king, his fame spread wide, Kings sent their envoys to sit by his side.
Hiram, king of Tyre, sent word to his friend, He heard Solomon's reign had come to commence. Loved David, he did, with a loyal heart, Sent messengers swiftly, playing his part.
Solomon spoke, sent a message back, "My father David, he faced attack, Couldn't build a house for Yahweh's name, Too many wars, too much to claim.
But now God's given me peace and rest, No enemies here, no threats to test. I plan to build that house so grand, Just like Yahweh promised, by His hand.
I need your cedar from Lebanon's tall, My servants will help, just give the call. Your Sidonians, the best with the trees, No one cuts timber with such ease."
Hiram heard Solomon and joy did rise, "Blessed be Yahweh, wise son under skies. I'll do your will, send cedar and more, Cypress rafts to your designated shore.
In return, bring food, my household's need, We'll trade in peace, in thought and deed." So timber flowed to Solomon's land, And food and oil went by Solomon's hand.
Yahweh gave Solomon wisdom deep, Peace with Hiram, a treaty to keep. A levy of men, thirty thousand strong, To Lebanon they went, a month not long.
Seventy thousand bore burdens great, Eighty thousand stone cutters, fate. The leaders, three thousand and three hundred more, Ruling over laborers, building Yahweh's floor.
They cut large stones, precious and rare, To lay the foundation with utmost care. Builders from Solomon, Hiram, and Gebal, Together they worked, to raise that hall.

Yo, four hundred and eighty years after Egypt's release, In Solomon's fourth year, he started the piece. Month of Ziv, the second one, time to begin, Yahweh's house rising, where His glory would spin.
Sixty cubits long, twenty wide, thirty high, Solomon built it to kiss the sky. The porch was twenty cubits long, ten wide, Fixed lattice windows to let light inside.
Against the walls, floors wrapped around, Temple and sanctuary, side rooms were found. Five, six, seven cubits, each floor grew, Beams offset, not to pierce through.
Quarry stones, no hammer's sound, Silent construction, sacred ground. Winding stairs, middle and third, Cedar beams, Yahweh's word heard:
"Walk in my statutes, keep my decree, I promise to dwell and never flee." So Solomon built, finished the task, Cedar boards inside, walls unmasked.
Cedar carvings, buds, flowers in bloom, All hidden stone, gold within the room. Ark set in the sanctuary, most holy space, Twenty cubits square, gold-covered place.
Cherubim of olive wood, wings spread wide, Touching walls, golden wings side by side. Every wall carved, cherubim, palms, flowers, Gold-covered floors, inside and outside towers.
Olive wood doors, carved, overlaid with gold, Cherubim and palms, stories told. Inner court, stone and cedar beams laid, Seven years in Bul, the house then displayed.
Solomon built a house, took thirteen years, Finished his crib, shed no tears.
A Forest of Lebanon, cedar and stone, Pillars and beams, like a king on a throne.
Covered in cedar, beams fifteen per row, Windows aligned, let the breezes flow.
Porch with pillars, fifty by thirty, A throne of judgment, never dirty.
His own pad and Pharaoh’s daughter's too, Cedar and costly stones shaping the view.
Foundation laid with mighty stones, Ten cubits, eight cubits—each one honed.
Cedar beams and costly fair, Three courses of stones lined with care.
Summoned was Hiram, bronze in his hand, Skilled, wise, a worker so grand.
Bronze pillars rose, eighteen cubits tall, Caps of five cubits, gracing them all.
Checker work, chains, around they twine, Lily work capitals, oh so fine.
Pillars named Jachin and Boaz in place, Lily tops finished with style and grace.
A sea of bronze, ten cubits wide, Twelve oxen beneath, as if they guide.
Thick as a hand, brim like a cup, Held two thousand baths, filled right up.
Ten bases made, four cubits in length, Panels with lions showing their strength.
Wheels of bronze, like chariots they rolled, Solid as stone, their story told.
Each base with cherubim, palm trees, and more, A uniform casting, a measured score.
Ten basins of bronze, forty baths each, Set side by side within easy reach.
Hiram molded pots, shovels, and basins, Bronze work for the Lord’s holy places.
Two pillars, bowls, networks, ornate, Four hundred pomegranates to decorate.
Bases, basins, sea with twelve oxen, All burnished bronze, polished like toxin.
Cast in the Jordan's clay grounds, So many vessels, their weight unbound.
Golden altar and table for bread, Lamp stands shining, glowing ahead.
Gold cups, snuffers, basins, and more, For the inner house of the Lord to adore.
Finished was all Solomon's glorious task, Treasures of David in Yahweh's house, at last.

Solomon called the elders, they all came to the scene, In Jerusalem, for the ark, it was time to convene. The whole of Israel gathered in the seventh month, To bring the ark of Yahweh's covenant upfront.

Priests and Levites lifted the ark up high, With holy vessels from the Tent, reaching for the sky. Sheep and cattle sacrificed, uncountable, immense, Before the holy ark, making Israel's presence intense.

The priests set the ark in the sanctuary, its sacred dome, Under the wings of cherubim, the ark found its home. Long poles peeking from the holy space, yet unseen, Only the tablets of the covenant, kept pristine.

As priests exited, a cloud filled Yahweh's abode, His glory so dense, they couldn't bear the load. Solomon spoke, "Yahweh dwells in darkness thick, I've built Your house forever, where Your light will stick."

He turned to Israel, blessed them, and they stood, "Praise Yahweh," he declared, "for keeping promises good." From Egypt to now, no city was chosen, But David was made king, the divine plan not frozen.

David dreamed of a house for Yahweh's name, But God chose his son to bring that dream to fame. "Yahweh's word is true," Solomon declared with pride, "I built this house, where His covenant does reside."
Hands raised to heaven, Solomon began to pray, Acknowledging Yahweh's greatness every single day. "Keep promises to David, let his line hold strong, If his children walk right and avoid the wrong."

"Can heaven itself contain God?" Solomon mused, Yet he asked for God’s ears, towards their prayers fused. "When people sin and face the enemy's might, If they turn here and pray, make their wrongs right."

"If the skies hold back rain, famine strikes the land, Hear their prayers, teach them, let them understand. Foreigners too, who come to honor Your fame, Hear them from heaven, so they know Your name."
"If captives repent, far from home they stay, Hear their cries and maintain their way. For they are Yours, Your treasured claim, Brought out of Egypt, by Your mighty name."
Solomon finished, rose from his knees, Blessed the assembly, as they felt at ease. "Yahweh's words never fail, He's with us this day, May our hearts follow Him, in His statutes, we’ll stay."
Sacrifices offered, in abundance they came, Dedicating Yahweh’s house, all in His name. Fourteen days of feast, joy spread wide and far, The people went home, with gladness in their hearts.
Solomon finished building with grand design, Yahweh’s house and the king’s combined. Yahweh appeared once more, as he'd done before, in a moment divine, at Gibeon’s door.
He said, “I've heard your prayer, to set my name there. This house is made holy, with my eyes and heart, I’ll forever care.”
“Walk like David did, with integrity and might, Keep my statutes and commandments in your sight.”
“I’ll establish your throne, your kingdom will never fall, As David was promised, so it shall be for all.”
“But turn away from me, and serve gods not true, I’ll cut Israel off, and cast away this view.”
“Though the house stands tall, strangers will scorn and laugh, They’ll wonder why this land suffers Yahweh’s wrath.”
“They’ll say, ‘Because they left Yahweh, who freed their kin, Embraced other gods, so this destruction came in.’”
Twenty years passed by, two houses Solomon made, With cedar, cypress, and gold, by Hiram's aid.
Solomon gifted Hiram cities of Galilee, Hiram didn’t like them, “Cabul” they’d be.
With gold he sent, one hundred twenty fold, For all the work and the stories told.
Pharaoh’s forces took Gezer by fire and sword, A wedding gift to Solomon's bride, Egypt's accord.
Solomon built up cities and storage space, For horses and chariots, across the place.
People left from old tribes, not Israel’s sons, Made bondservants still, from battles not won.
Israel's children weren’t servants, they were warriors brave, Chiefs over labor, in the work they gave.
Pharaoh’s daughter moved to a house built anew, Solomon constructed Millo, as he was due.
He offered sacrifices on Yahweh’s altar, Three times a year, his faith didn’t falter.
Solomon built a fleet by the Red Sea’s shore, Hiram’s sailors joined, with knowledge galore.
They traveled to Ophir, fetching gold so bright, Four hundred twenty talents, a treasure in sight.
Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame, Came with questions, testing his name. Caravan of spices, gold, and stones, In Jerusalem, she laid out her tones.
Solomon answered, nothing stayed hidden, His wisdom revealed, her doubts were overridden. She saw his house, his table spread wide, Servants in splendor, her wonder magnified.
"No more spirit," in awe she cried, "Reports I heard, and truth wasn't denied. Not half was told, your wisdom's grand, Happy are those who in your court stand.
Blessed be Yahweh, who set you high, To rule with justice, under the sky." She gave him gold, spices in great measure, Never again such spices, a rare treasure.
Hiram's fleet brought almug trees, For the house and the king's harmonies. Solomon granted her every desire, To her own land, she did retire.
Gold flowed in, six sixty-six talents a year, From traders, merchants, governors near. Bucklers and shields of beaten gold, In the Forest of Lebanon, a sight to behold.
A throne of ivory, gold overlaid, With lions beside, a grand parade. Twelve lions on steps, never seen before, Solomon's kingdom, a legend and lore.
Drinking vessels of gold, silver held no sway, Riches and wisdom, his every day. Fleet of Tarshish, treasures did bring, Solomon's name, the earth did sing.
Chariots and horsemen, cities filled, Silver like stones, Jerusalem thrilled. Horses from Egypt, merchants did trade, To kings afar, deals they made.
Solomon loved women from every land, Though God warned Israel, "Don't take their hand.
"They'll turn your heart to other gods," He'd say, But Solomon loved them anyway.
Seven hundred wives, concubines a ton, They turned his heart, and Yahweh said, "You're done."
He chased after Ashtoreth and Milcom’s call, Didn't follow Yahweh, did what was appall.
Built high places for Chemosh and Molech's game, For his foreign wives, he bowed to their flame.
Yahweh was angry, His heart filled with pain, For Solomon forgot God's word again.
"Didn't I appear to you once, then twice? Commanded you to follow, but you paid the price.
"For this, I'll tear the kingdom from your hand, Give it to your servant, like shifting sand.
"Won't do it in your day, for David's sake, But your son's reign will surely break.
"One tribe for David, my servant's light, For Jerusalem, my chosen in the night."
Adversaries rose, Hadad came to fight, Once a child in Egypt, returned with might.
Rezon the rebel gathered a crew, Hated Israel, made trouble anew.
Jeroboam stood, a mighty man of fame, Solomon saw his strength, knew his name.
Ahijah the prophet tore his robe in two, Gave ten pieces, "These tribes are for you."
Yahweh's words echoed, "You'll reign, if you heed, Walk in my ways, and succeed.
"I'll build you a house, steadfast and true, Afflict David's line, but not forever, too."
Solomon sought Jeroboam’s end in sight, But he fled to Egypt, stayed out of the fight.
Solomon's deeds, his wisdom full of praise, Written in the book of his days.
Forty years he reigned, then took his rest, Rehoboam his son, continued the quest.
Rehoboam came to Shechem, aiming to be crowned king, Israel gathered round, ready for the offering.
Jeroboam heard the news while in Egypt, he had fled, Came back with the people, this is what he said:
“Your father was harsh, gave us a heavy load, Lighten our burden, and our loyalty will be bestowed.”
Rehoboam said, “Give me three days, then return,” He sought counsel, wisdom to discern.
Old men advised, “Serve the people, speak with care, Do this today, and they'll always be there.”
But he turned to the young, who grew by his side, “What should I say?” he asked, setting wisdom aside.
The young men replied, “Tell them this tale, ‘My finger’s thicker than my father’s scale.’
‘My father whipped you, but with scorpions I'll reign, I'll add to your burdens, feel my disdain.’”
On the third day, the people returned to the king’s court, He spoke roughly, ignoring wisdom's report.
“My father was harsh, but I’ll be more severe, He used whips, but scorpions you'll fear.”
The people saw the king wouldn’t heed their plea, Broke from David’s line, shouting, “Israel, be free!”
Rehoboam ruled Judah, but the rest split away, Sent Adoram, but stoning marked the fray.
Rehoboam fled, rushed to Jerusalem's gate, Israel rebelled, dividing the state.
Jeroboam became king, Israel’s new pride, Only Judah remained by Rehoboam’s side.
God spoke through Shemaiah, His command clear, “Don’t fight your brothers, this division must adhere.”
Jeroboam built altars, calves of gold to bow, “Don’t go up to Jerusalem, worship here now.”
In Bethel and Dan, idols stood tall, People sinned, heedless to God’s call.
Priests from the people, not Levi’s line, Jeroboam’s feast, his own design.
Sacrifices made in his crafted place, Worshiping idols, forgetting God’s grace.
A man of God from Judah came to Bethel land, Jeroboam at the altar, incense in his hand. He cried out loud, “Oh altar, hear Yahweh’s decree, A son named Josiah will bring priests to their knees."
He gave a sign, the altar would split wide, Ashes pouring out, with nowhere to hide. The king heard the word, and stretched his hand, “Seize him!” he commanded, a fractured demand.
But his hand shriveled up, frozen in place, Couldn't pull it back, left in disgrace. The altar split, ashes poured on the ground, The sign of Yahweh, His power renowned.
The king pleaded, “Pray for me, let my hand be restored,” The man of God prayed, and Yahweh’s grace poured. The hand was healed, as good as new, The king offered gifts, “Come, refresh with my crew.”
But the man of God said, “No way, no bread, Yahweh told me ‘fast,’ I’ll obey what He said.” He took a different path, obeying the route, Not returning the way he came, no doubt.
An old prophet in Bethel heard the tale, His sons told him all, they didn’t fail. “Which way did he go?” the prophet did ask, On a donkey he rode, a determined task.
He found the man under an oak tree's shade, “Come home with me, let’s feast,” he bade. But the man of God stayed firm to his word, “Yahweh’s command is all I’ve heard.”
The old prophet lied, “An angel did speak, ‘Bring him back, let him eat, let him drink.’” So he went back, breaking the vow, In the prophet's home, he ate bread now.
At the table, Yahweh’s voice came to the liar, Spoke to the man, words of dire fire, “For breaking command, you’ll die on the road, Your body alone, not in father’s abode.”
After the meal, he saddled his ride, A lion met him, and there he died. The donkey and lion stood by the slain, Men passed by, saw the body, felt the pain.
The old prophet heard, “It’s the man, disobeyed, Yahweh's word, now he's slayed.” He found the body, lion still on guard, Took him home, the prophet's heart scarred.
Laid him in his own grave, mournful cries, “Alas, my brother,” with teary eyes. He told his sons, “When my life is done, Lay me beside him, our bones as one.”
The king didn't change, kept walking in sin, Made high place priests, the trouble within. This sin cut off Jeroboam's line, Destroyed his house, a judgment divine.
Abijah got sick, Jeroboam felt the heat, Told his wife, "Disguise, don’t let them see your feet. Head to Shiloh, where Ahijah stays, Take loaves, cakes, honey, listen to what he says.”
She did as told, journeyed with care, Ahijah, blind but knew she'd be there. God whispered to him, “Jeroboam’s wife will come, Pretending she's another, but let’s not play dumb.”
She walked through the door, he didn’t miss a beat, “Come in, Jeroboam’s wife, take a seat. Heavy news I bring, straight from the Lord, ‘Cause you turned from the path, ignored His accord.”
"You were lifted up, made king of this land, But turned to idols, provoked by your hand. So your house will fall, swept away like waste, Dogs and birds will feast, such is your fate.”
“When you step back home, your child will die, Israel will mourn, tears they won’t deny. A new king will rise, Jeroboam’s line will fail, Israel shaken, scattered like a gale.”
She left Ahijah, with a heavy heart, Reached home’s threshold, her son did depart. Israel mourned, just as the word had been, Written in chronicles, of what had been seen.
Jeroboam reigned, twenty-two years long, Then he rested, his son carried on. Rehoboam ruled Judah, with sin in its sight, Idols and high places, under every tree’s light.
In his fifth year, Egypt’s king came, Took treasures of gold, left Judah in shame. Bronze shields replaced what was once gold’s gleam, Wars raged on, like a recurring theme.
Rehoboam passed, laid with his own, Abijam took the throne, his legacy shown. The tales of kings, their deeds and their fate, Written in chronicles, a history's weight.
In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's time, Abijam reigned Judah, his mountain to climb. Three years in Jerusalem, he held his throne, Maacah's son, but his sins were his own.
Not like David, his heart wasn't right, Yet for David's sake, God held the light. A lamp in the city, a son to succeed, Jerusalem's strength, a legacy indeed.
War raged on between Rehoboam's line, The chronicles tell of Abijam's time. He slept with his fathers, in peace he lay, Asa his son took the throne that day.
In Jeroboam's twentieth, Asa ruled strong, Forty-one years in a city where kings belong. He did what was right in the sight of the Lord, Cleared the idols, broke the sinful cord.
Maacah removed, her image he burned, At Kidron's brook, her power spurned. Though high places stood, Asa's heart was true, Silver and gold to the temple he drew.
War with Baasha, Israel's king, Ramah built up, a siege it would bring. Asa sought help, sent gifts of gold, To Ben Hadad in Syria, alliances bold.
"Break with Baasha," Asa's decree, Ben Hadad struck cities, setting Asa free. Ramah abandoned, its stones Asa claimed, Building up Judah, his strength proclaimed.
The chronicles tell of Asa's feats, But old age brought pain to his feet. Asa slept with his fathers, his reign complete, Jehoshaphat rose, Judah's new beat.
Nadab ruled Israel, Asa's second year, But his evil deeds brought Baasha near. Baasha struck him down, claiming the crown, Jeroboam's house, he tore it down.
Baasha's reign, like Jeroboam's sin, Provoked God's anger from deep within. The chronicles hold their deeds and fights, Through Asa and Baasha, enduring nights.

Yahweh's word came strong, to Jehu it was sent, "From dust I raised you up, as Israel's prince you were meant. But you walked like Jeroboam, made my people stray, Provoked my anger, so your house I'll sweep away.
Dogs will feast on those in the city who fall, Birds will devour the rest beyond the wall." Baasha's deeds and might, in chronicles they write, He slept where his fathers lay, Elah took the right.
Yahweh spoke again to Jehu, prophet's call, Baasha's house of sin, destined to fall. In Asa's twenty-sixth year, Elah took the throne, For two years he reigned, but wasn't left alone.

Zimri, captain bold, conspired in Tirzah's night, Elah drank and stumbled, Zimri seized the fight. He struck him down in Asa's twenty-seventh year, Claimed the throne for himself, but brought more fear.
Zimri wiped Baasha's kin, just like Yahweh said, For sins they laid on Israel, in vanities they led. Elah's record, deeds all noted down, In chronicles of Israel's kings, where stories abound.
Zimri's rule short-lived, just seven days in fame, Omri rose with Israel's might, laid claim to the name. Tirzah besieged, Zimri saw the fall, Into fire he went, his sins recalled.
Israel's hearts divided, Omri or Tibni's way, Omri's strength prevailed, Tibni's end in dismay. Omri reigned in Samaria, twelve years' span, Built the city up, Samaria began.

But he walked in Jeroboam's path, evil in Yahweh's sight, Provoked the Lord's anger, with vanities of night. Chronicles hold his might, his deeds in view, Omri slept with fathers, Ahab's reign was due.
Ahab took the throne, wickedness increased, Married Jezebel, Baal worship's feast. Built altars high, God's anger he did stir, More than kings before him, his sins did incur.
In those days Hiel built Jericho again, At the cost of sons, his heart knew pain. Fulfilled the word spoken long ago, By Joshua's mouth, Jericho's woe.
Elijah the Tishbite, bold and brave, Spoke to Ahab, no rain, no dew to save. "As Yahweh lives, before whom I stand, No rain till I command it in this land."
God's word came, "Head east, don't stay, Hide by Cherith brook, that's the way. Drink from its flow, the ravens will feed, Bread and meat twice daily, that's your need."
Elijah obeyed, lived by the brook's side, Ravens brought food, his needs supplied. But soon the brook ran dry, no rain to fall, Then Yahweh's word came with a new call.
"Arise, go to Zarephath, Sidon's place, A widow I've chosen, to sustain you with grace." He went to the city, saw her gathering there, "Bring me some water," he asked with care.
"And a morsel of bread," he added on, But she said, "I have barely any, it's almost gone. Just a handful of meal, a little oil in a jar, After this meal, death won't be far."
Elijah reassured her, "Don't be afraid, First make me a cake, as I have said. For Yahweh says, your supplies won't deplete, Until rain falls again, your kitchen's replete."
She obeyed his words, and many days they ate, Meal and oil didn't run out, it was fate. But her son grew ill, breath ceased in his chest, She cried to Elijah, her heart in distress.
Elijah said, "Give me your son," took him up high, Laid him on his bed, pleaded with God on high. "Yahweh, bring back this child's soul," he cried, Three times he stretched, no breath denied.
God heard Elijah, brought life back anew, Elijah brought him down, "Behold, he lives, it's true!" The woman exclaimed, her faith now strong and clear, "You're a man of God, your words I hold dear."
Yo, after many days, Yahweh's word came through, Told Elijah, "Show yourself to Ahab, rain's due." The famine was fierce, Samaria was dry, Elijah set his sights on Ahab, said bye-bye.
Ahab called Obadiah, his right-hand man, Obadiah feared Yahweh, had a prophet-saving plan. Jezebel cut prophets like a villain in the night, Obadiah hid a hundred, kept 'em out of sight.
Ahab said, “Search the land, find us some grass, Save the horses and mules, make our resources last.” Dividing paths, Ahab and Obadiah split ways, Obadiah met Elijah, and was amazed.
"Is it you, my lord Elijah?" he bowed down low, Elijah said, "It is I, go and let Ahab know." Obadiah shook his head, fear in his eyes, "If I say you're here, and then you fly, I might die."
But Elijah stood firm, "As Yahweh lives," he said, "I'll show myself to Ahab, no need for dread." Obadiah told Ahab, who met Elijah quick, Ahab called him trouble, but Elijah came back slick.
"I ain't troubled Israel, it's you and your kin, Forsaken Yahweh, let Baal's worship begin." "Gather all Israel to Mount Carmel's peak, Four fifty prophets of Baal, and more from Jezebel's clique."
Ahab gathered them all, the prophets in line, Elijah stepped up, his voice like a chime. "How long will you waver, between two paths? If Yahweh's God, follow Him, or face His wrath."
Elijah took two bulls, laid the challenge down, "Call your god’s name, I'll call Yahweh’s renown. Let the one who sends fire be the true divine, People agreed, "This idea's mighty fine."
Baal’s prophets danced, called from morning till noon, But the heavens stayed silent, no voice in tune. Elijah teased, "Maybe Baal's on a trip, Cry louder, wake him up, get him to flip."
No answer came, even as blood spilled, Prophets of Baal stood there, hopes unfulfilled. Elijah called the people, gathered them near, Repaired Yahweh's altar, said, "Come here."
Twelve stones, one for each tribe, he took with care, Built an altar, Yahweh's name in the air. Filled jars with water, soaked the altar all through, "Do it again," then a third time too.
Water flowed, filling trenches wide, Elijah stepped forth, no fear to hide. "Yahweh, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel," he prayed, "Show them your power, let their hearts be swayed."
Fire fell from heaven, a consuming blaze, Burned offering, wood, stones, in a mighty craze. People fell on faces, shouted loud and broad, "Yahweh, He is God! Yahweh, He is God!"

Elijah called, "Seize Baal's prophets, not one to flee," Took them to Kishon, ended them decisively. To Ahab, Elijah said, "Get up, eat, and drink, For the sound of rain approaches, making you think."
Ahab dined, while Elijah climbed to the top, Prayed with face to knees, no plan to stop. Sent his servant to look toward the sea's rim, On the seventh try, a cloud appeared slim.

"Tell Ahab, 'Get ready, rain is on the way,'" Sky turned black, clouds gathered, with no delay. Elijah tucked his cloak, with Yahweh's strength he ran, Before Ahab to Jezreel, speed like a whirlwind fan.
Ahab told Jezebel, "Elijah's done a feat, He struck down prophets, made their end complete." Jezebel sent a threat, hot as a flame, "By tomorrow, Elijah, your fate will be the same."
Elijah heard this and ran for his life, To Beersheba he went, escaping the strife. Alone in the wilderness, under the tree, He begged the Lord, "Take my life, let me be."
He lay down in despair but wasn't alone, An angel tapped him, with a voice like a tone, "Arise and eat," the angel softly said, A cake and water waited by his head.
He ate and drank, then lay down again, The angel returned, "The journey's not plain. Arise and eat, for the road is long, In this strength, you must be strong."
Forty days, forty nights, to Horeb’s height, Elijah walked with God's might. In a cave he found rest, in the mountain deep, Then Yahweh spoke to him, waking him from sleep,
"What are you doing here, Elijah, my man?" "I've been zealous, but they break your plan. Israel's lost, your altars they razed, I'm the last, and they're seeking my days."
"Stand on the mountain, see Yahweh pass by." Wind tore the mountains, rocks broke and flew high. But Yahweh wasn't in the wind or in the quake, Nor in the fire did His voice awake.
A still small voice in the silence came, Elijah heard it, wrapped his face in shame. "What are you doing here?" the voice asked again, Elijah poured out his heart, his pain.
"Return to Damascus, the wilderness way, Anoint Hazael and Jehu without delay. Elisha shall follow, in your prophetic place, Seven thousand I've kept who have not turned their face."
Elijah moved on, found Elisha at the plow, Placed his mantle on him, made the sacred vow. Elisha said, "Let me bid my family goodbye." Elijah nodded, "Go on, don't ask why."
Elisha returned, the oxen were slain, He fed the people, broke every chain. Then he rose up, followed Elijah's track, Together they went, not looking back.

Ben Hadad gathered his force, thirty-two kings by his side, Chariots and horses, ready for a fierce ride. Samaria was besieged, Ahab faced the threat, A message was sent, "Your silver, gold, don't forget.
"Your wives, your children, the best you possess, Hand them over," was Ben Hadad's request. Ahab replied, "All I have, it's yours, my king," But Ben Hadad's demands, they had a nasty ring.
"You'll hand it all over, tomorrow they'll take, Search your houses, whatever they like, they'll rake." Ahab called his elders, "This man craves more, Our silver and gold, he seeks to score."
Elders and people, they all took a stand, "Don't listen, don't consent to his demand." Ahab sent word, "The first I will do, But to all your demands, I can't be true."
Ben Hadad replied, "The gods curse me more, If Samaria's dust isn't enough for my war." Ahab said, "Don't boast as you put armor on, Like you would when the battle's been won."
Ben Hadad drank, prepared to attack, While a prophet approached Ahab, ready to crack. "Yahweh says, 'This multitude, in your hand I'll place, So you'll know I'm Yahweh, giver of grace.'"
"By whom?" Ahab asked, and the prophet said, "By the young princes, they'll take the lead ahead." Two hundred thirty-two young men stood tall, And all of Israel answered the call.
At noon they marched, while Ben Hadad drank, The princes went first, Ben Hadad's confidence sank. "If for peace or war, take them alive," Yet Israel's youth began to strive.
Each struck his man, Syrians fled and ran, Ben Hadad escaped, his royal plan in sand. Israel struck hard, horses and chariots fell, With a great slaughter, they made Syrians dwell.
The prophet returned, said to Ahab, "Get strong, For Syria again will come before long." Syria's servants plotted, "We'll fight on the plain, Their god rules hills, but here we'll reign."
New captains, new ranks, horses and chariots amassed, They faced Israel, the countryside was vast. Yet like young goats, Israel stood small, Against Syrian might, they'd answer the call.

A man of God spoke, "Yahweh says to you, 'Though they think I'm a hill god, I'll prove it's not true.'" For seven days they camped, then war they did wage, Israel killed a hundred thousand, set the stage.

The rest fled, walls fell, twenty-seven thousand crushed, Ben Hadad hid, his escape was hushed. His servants said, "Beg for mercy, for Israel's kings show grace," Wrapped in sackcloth, they sought Ahab's face.
"Let me live," Ben Hadad pleaded with plea, Ahab called him "brother," set him free. Cities restored, treaties made anew, Ahab let him go, the deal bid adieu.
A prophet disguised, a test for the king, In the battlefield's midst, a tale he did bring. "He was gone," the servant said, busy he had been, The king passed judgment, his own words came in.
The prophet revealed, his disguise cast away, "Yahweh's word, your life now must pay." Ahab went home, sullen and mad, From victory's joy, his ending was sad.
Naboth had a vineyard, right next to the king, Ahab saw it, thought, "A garden it could bring."
"Let me have your vines," the king did plea, "I'll pay or trade, whichever suits thee."
Naboth said, "No, it's my father's land," Yahweh forbids the deal you demand."
Ahab went home, sour and alone, Lay on his bed, face to the stone.
Jezebel came, asked, "Why the long face?" Ahab replied, "Naboth's put me in place."
Jezebel said, "Aren't you the king? Rise and dine, I'll make that vineyard yours, just give it time."
She wrote letters, sealed with the king's name, To elders and nobles, playing a cruel game.
"Proclaim a fast, set Naboth high, Have two scoundrels say he cursed the Most High."
The city elders did what she planned, They stoned Naboth by Jezebel's hand.
"He's dead," they said, "now claim your prize," Jezebel told Ahab, "Open your eyes."
Ahab rose up, to the vineyard he'd tread, But Elijah came with words to dread.
Yahweh's voice spoke through the prophet's shout, "You've killed and taken, so here's your route."
"Dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they'll lick yours too, For the evil things that you pursue."
Ahab cried, "My enemy, you've found me now!" Elijah said, "Yes, for evil you allow."
"I'll cut you off, your house will fall, Like Jeroboam's, no one left at all."
"Jezebel's fate? Dogs will feast, In Jezreel, they'll eat her piece by piece."
Ahab repented, tore his clothes in despair, Put on sackcloth, walked with care.
Yahweh saw him humble, and said with grace, "No evil now, but in your son’s place."
Three years of peace, no war in sight, Jehoshaphat came down, ready to unite. Israel’s king said, "Ramoth Gilead's ours, But we do nothing, let’s reclaim our powers."

He asked Jehoshaphat, "Will you fight by my side?" Jehoshaphat replied, "Our forces will ride." "But first," he said, "Let's seek Yahweh’s command," Prophets gathered, four hundred strong, in the land.

"Go to battle," they said, "It’s yours to take," Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there a true voice for Yahweh’s sake?" "There’s Micaiah," Israel's king confessed, "But his words bring me distress, not blessed."
"Bring him here," said the king with demand, While the prophets prophesied, iron horns in hand. Zedekiah shouted, "With these you'll win," The messenger nudged Micaiah, "Speak like them, begin."
Micaiah declared, "Yahweh’s words I’ll speak," The king asked, "From truth don’t you dare sneak." Micaiah said, "Israel’s scattered like sheep, No master, back to their homes, in peace they seep."
The king groaned, "See, never good for me, Always evil, never setting me free." Yahweh's vision Micaiah shared loud, "Heaven's army, Yahweh’s questions, proud."
"Who'll entice Ahab?" Yahweh asked the throng, A spirit stepped up, "I’ll make it wrong." "Go," Yahweh said, "deceive with might," Now the prophets’ words fall from Yahweh’s sight.
Zedekiah struck, "Yahweh, where'd you go?" "Hidden you'll see," Micaiah replied slow. The king ordered, "Take him, locked away, Bread and water of affliction, till I return day."
"If you come back," Micaiah's words rang, "Yahweh didn’t speak, hear the clang." Into battle they marched, kings side by side, Israel's king disguised, in robes Jehoshaphat complied.
Syria’s orders: "Only the king to fight," They chased Jehoshaphat, then turned in flight. A bow at random, hit Israel's king, "Wounded, take me away," his voice did sing.
Propped in his chariot, the king met his fate, Blood pooled as the sun set late. "Return to your homes," the cry did say, In Samaria, Ahab was laid that day.
Chariot washed, dogs licked his blood, As Yahweh spoke, there was no flood. Ahab's deeds in chronicles written down, Ahaziah reigned next, taking the crown.
Jehoshaphat walked in the path of his kin, Doing right in Yahweh's eyes, but high places didn’t dim. Ships to Ophir wrecked on the way, Ahaziah asked to join, but Jehoshaphat said nay.
Jehoshaphat slept, legacy sustained, Jehoram his son, now reigned and remained. Ahaziah did evil, Baal he served, Provoking Yahweh's wrath, justice reserved.

Moab's rebellion hit the scene, after Ahab's death, they weren't keen. Ahaziah stumbled, through the lattice he fell, sick in Samaria, feeling unwell. He sent his messengers on a quest, to inquire of Baal Zebub, was his health blessed? But Yahweh's angel whispered to the Tishbite, "Go meet those messengers, set the story right."

"Why seek Ekron's god when Israel's is near?" "Yahweh declares, 'You won't leave your bed, death is here.'" Elijah told the messengers, then left them behind, Back to the king, with words that were divine.
The king asked, "Why back so fast?" They spoke of a man with a message to cast, "Yahweh's words were firm and real, There's no escape from the fate you feel."
"What kind of man?" was the king's demand. "A hairy man, leather belt in hand." "That's Elijah," the king huffed with a frown, Sent his captain with fifty, to bring Elijah down.
"Man of God, the king calls you, come on down!" Elijah replied, "Let fire rain, consume this town!" And fire roared down, burned them to ash, The king sent more, but they met the same crash.
A third captain came, his knees hit the ground, "Man of God, spare us, let life abound!" Fire had toasted those who came before, "Please spare us, let us live once more."
Angel of Yahweh said, "Elijah, go, Don't be afraid, with this man flow." Elijah went down, to the king he did speak, "You sought Baal Zebub, your fate is bleak."
"You'll not rise, but surely die," And as Yahweh spoke, Ahaziah's time ran dry. Jehoram took the throne, his reign would begin, Ahaziah's tale ended, written in chronicles within.
Elijah knew his time was near, a whirlwind ride to heaven's sphere, With Elisha at his side, from Gilgal they took the stride.
"Stay here," Elijah said, "for Yahweh calls me ahead." Elisha vowed, "I won't leave, as Yahweh lives, that's my creed."
Prophets in Bethel warned Elisha, "Today your master leaves ya." He nodded, "I know, keep it low," as they continued the flow.
Again Elijah spoke, "To Jericho, Yahweh beckons me to go." Elisha replied, "I'm with you, through and through, you know it's true."
Jericho's prophets said, "Elijah's leaving, your leader's head." "Yes, I know," Elisha replied, "but let's keep this on the quiet side."
"To the Jordan I must go," Elijah said, but Elisha wouldn't let go. Together they walked, prophets watched from afar, their faith locked.
Elijah's cloak smacked the river wide, and dry ground appeared side by side. On the other bank, Elijah turned, "Ask me now, before I'm spurned."
Elisha asked for a double share, of the spirit that Elijah's care. "It's a hard request," Elijah confessed, "but if you see me, you'll be blessed."
As they walked, fire from the sky, chariots and horses, Elijah flew high. "My father!" Elisha cried, torn robes in despair, as Elijah was in the air.
He picked the mantle, a legacy's sign, struck the waters, "Where's Yahweh divine?" The river split again, Elisha crossed, prophets saw the spirit wasn't lost.
"The spirit of Elijah's on Elisha," they bowed down, respect they show. "Send men to find him," they said, but Elisha declined, "He's gone ahead."
Pressed by their plea, he relented, "Go see," but three days passed without decree. "I told you not to go," Elisha said, as they returned with weary tread.
The city's water was bad, the land, a desolate span. Elisha called for a jar, with salt, to heal it near and far.
"Yahweh says, 'These waters are healed,'" Elisha declared, and the curse was repealed. To Bethel he went, mocked by youth, "Go up, baldy!" was their uncouth.
He cursed them in Yahweh's name, and bears came, their wrath untamed. Elisha continued, from Carmel to Samaria, led by Yahweh's aria.
Jehoram took the throne, son of Ahab's might, Eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, he reigned in sight. Twelve years he ruled, doing evil, it's true, But he tore down Baal's pillar, a different view.
Still clung to Jeroboam’s sin, wouldn’t depart, The legacy of Israel's wayward heart. Mesha the Moabite had sheep to spare, A hundred thousand lambs, a king's share.
But when Ahab died, Mesha turned, Against Israel's rule, his heart burned. Jehoram mustered all Israel, no time to slack, Called to Jehoshaphat, planning their track.
"The king of Moab's rebelled, join me in fight?" Jehoshaphat said, "I am with you, all right." "Which way shall we march?" Jehoram did say, "The wilderness of Edom," was the chosen way.
Three kings marching, seven days, yet dry, No water for the armies, the livestock nearby. The king of Israel cried, "Yahweh’s plan is grim, To deliver us three to Moab's hand within."
Jehoshaphat asked, "A prophet, can he be found?" "Elisha, who served Elijah, he's around." The kings went to Elisha, their hopes pinned, He said, "Go to your folks’ prophets, I’m disinclined."
But for Jehoshaphat, Elisha would heed, "Bring a musician," for Yahweh’s word to seed. "Yahweh says, 'Dig trenches, make them deep, No wind or rain, but water you’ll reap.'"
"This is easy for Yahweh, Moab's yours to claim, Strike every city, and shatter their flame." As morning came, water flowed in sight, A miracle in the valley, clear and bright.
Moab saw the water, red as blood, "Kings are dead," they thought, "we’ll plunder the flood!" But Israel rose and struck them down, Moab fled, Israel took the crown.
Every city fell, each land filled with stones, Springs were stopped, trees cut to bones. King of Moab, desperate, sacrifice his kin, Great wrath rose, Israel went home, within.
A wife cried to Elisha, "My husband is gone, you see, Feared the Lord, but now a creditor threatens my family." Elisha asked, "Tell me, what do you possess?" "Only a pot of oil," she confessed.
"Go, borrow vessels, every neighbor you can reach, Not just a few; let that be my teach. Close the door, pour the oil, don't hesitate, Fill each one, set aside, don't be late."
She did as he said, doors shut tight, Poured oil till every vessel was full, a miraculous sight. "No more containers," her son declared, And the flow ceased, just as she feared.
She told Elisha, the man of God spoke, "Sell the oil, pay your debt, live on the stroke."
Then Elisha journeyed to Shunem's place, A woman gave him bread, a warm embrace. She said to her man, "Let's build him a room, With a bed, a chair, and a lamp to light the gloom."

Elisha asked, "What can be done for your care?" Gehazi said, "She has no son, her husband's old, a rare affair." Elisha called her, "Next year, a son you'll hold," She replied, "Don't lie, don't be bold."
But true were the words, a son she bore, Years passed, the child grew, loved even more. One day, "My head!" cried the boy in pain, Carried to his mother, where he lay till life wane.
She placed him on the man of God's bed, Mounted a donkey, "To Elisha," she said. "Why go today?" her husband inquired, "It's all right," she assured, not tired.
She reached Elisha on Mount Carmel high, "Is all well?" he asked, she answered nigh. Fell at his feet, "Don't deceive, did I plead?" Gehazi couldn't wake the child, he failed in the deed.
Elisha entered, shut the door, and prayed, Stretched on the child, the miracle displayed. The boy sneezed seven times, opened his eyes, Elisha called, "Now take your prize."
The mother bowed, thanked with tears and grace, She picked up her son, left the sacred space.
Famine struck, in Gilgal's land, Elisha ordered stew, no other demand. A wild vine’s gourds were gathered in haste, "Death in the pot!" the prophets cried, distaste.
"Bring meal!" Elisha threw it in, "Now serve the stew," the end of their din. Nothing harmful remained, God’s word held true, All ate and were filled, with plenty of stew.

A man came with barley bread, first fruits at hand, "Give it to the people," was Elisha’s command. "What, for a hundred?" the servant did protest, "They'll eat and have leftovers," Yahweh’s promise blessed.
The people ate their fill, with food left for later, In God’s provision, no one was a debater.
Naaman, a captain, mighty and grand, But leprosy marked him with a heavy hand. An Israelite girl, a captive, a maid, Said, "A prophet in Samaria could have him saved."
The news reached the king, who wrote with pride, Sent Naaman with gifts to the Israelite side. The king of Israel read, tore his robe in fear, "Am I God to heal? Why send Naaman here?"
Elisha, the prophet, heard the king's distress, "Send him to me, and I'll handle the rest." Naaman with chariots stood at Elisha's door, But a messenger came with instructions, nothing more.
"Go wash in the Jordan, seven times flow, Then you'll be clean; let your true colors show." Naaman was angry, "This can't be right! The rivers of Damascus put this Jordan to flight."
His servants spoke softly, "If he'd asked for more, Wouldn't you do it? Just try—there's hope in store." Down to the Jordan, Naaman dipped seven round, His skin renewed, like a child's, glory found.
Back to Elisha, with gratitude and awe, "There's no God but in Israel, so pure and raw. Take a gift from me, for the work you've done." But Elisha refused, "I take gifts from none."
Naaman asked for earth, two mules' worth, To worship Yahweh, the God of all earth. "Grant me pardon when my king bows in Rimmon's place," Elisha said, "Go in peace, and walk in grace."
But Gehazi, Elisha's servant, sought a prize, Chased after Naaman, with deceitful lies. "Give silver and garments," he asked with a grin, Naaman, generous, gave without chagrin.
Gehazi hid the goods, then faced Elisha's truth, "Where have you been?" Elisha asked, without sooth. "My heart went with you, saw the deceit you spun, Now Naaman's leprosy to you and your sons."
Gehazi left, his skin white as snow, Bearing the curse, reaping what he'd sow. Thus the tale of Naaman, in Israel's heart it stays, Of healing, deceit, and Elisha's unyielding ways.
The prophets to Elisha, "Our place is too tight, Let's head to the Jordan, build something right." "Go," he replied, "and take me along," To the Jordan they went, their axes swung strong.
As one chopped a tree, the ax head took flight, Into the water, out of sight. "Master, it's borrowed!" the man did wail, Elisha asked, "Where?" and then did prevail.
He cut a stick, threw it in, made iron float, "Take it," he said, and the man did tote. Syria's king plotted war's cunning plan, "Here we will camp," he told his clan.
Elisha warned Israel, "Avoid this place," The king of Israel moved with haste. The Syrian king was troubled, "Who’s the spy?" "No, Elisha hears what you speak and reply."

"Find him," the king commanded, "in Dothan he stays," With horses and chariots, they came by night’s haze. Elisha's servant saw the army, "What shall we do?" "Fear not," said Elisha, "we’ve more in view."
"Yahweh, open his eyes," Elisha did pray, He saw hills with fiery chariots array. Elisha prayed again, "Blind them, oh Lord," Struck with blindness, they knew not their ford.

"This is not the city," Elisha led them away, To Samaria's heart, then prayed, "Lord, let them see." The king of Israel asked, "Shall I strike them down?" "No," Elisha said, "let mercy wear the crown."
They feasted and drank, then sent them in peace, Syria’s raids on Israel ceased. Yet Benhadad besieged Samaria's gate, With famine so harsh, no food on the plate.
A woman cried out, "Help, oh king, relieve!" He replied, "If God won't help, what can I achieve?" She spoke of a pact, two sons to consume, Her tale of despair made the king’s heart fume.
He tore his clothes, sackcloth revealed, Vowed Elisha's fate would be sealed. With elders near, Elisha sat calm, A messenger sent with threats so strong.
"This evil is from Yahweh," the king’s cry, "Why should I wait?" with a heavy sigh. Elisha stood firm, faith in God's plan, Amidst chaos and threats, a resolute man.
Elisha spoke with a prophetic vibe, "Tomorrow flour’s gonna be real cheap, no jive.
The captain scoffed, doubting the divine, "If Heaven had windows, could it align?"
Four lepers sat at the city’s gate, "Why sit here, just accept our fate?
In the city, famine's got its grip, If we stay, we die, let’s take a trip.
Let’s head to the Syrians, see if they’re kind, If they save us, great, if not, we’re resigned."
At twilight they walked, hope on their side, To the Syrians’ camp, no soldiers to hide.
God had made sounds like a mighty, fierce raid, The Syrians fled fast, no time to parade.
Lepers found tents, gold, and silver to spare, They ate, drank, and hid treasures with care.
Then guilt struck their hearts, "This news is grand, Let’s tell the king, he'll understand."
They ran to the gatekeepers, shared what they saw, Syrians gone, but treasures and awe.
The king was cautious, "It’s a trap, I'm sure, The Syrians are hiding, they’ll lure us for sure."
A servant suggested, "Send scouts to see, What truth lies beyond, what reality?"
Chariots raced, found garments strewn, Syrians had fled, under the moon.
People rushed out, plundering the site, Flour and barley sold for a shekel, just right.
The captain, at the gate, trampled and gone, God’s word fulfilled, like Elisha had drawn.
The prophecy stood, every word was true, He saw the promise, but never tasted the view.
Elisha told the woman, "Get up, leave your home, Take your family, find a place where you can roam. For Yahweh decreed a famine, seven years it'll stay, Pack your things, head out without delay."

She listened, she moved, to the Philistines she went, Seven years passed, then back home she was sent. When she returned, her land she sought to claim, To the king she went, spoke her story, named her aim.
The king was chatting with Gehazi, the prophet's aide, Said, "Tell me ‘bout Elisha, all the miracles he made." Gehazi spoke of life restored, then lo and behold, The woman appeared, her story untold.
Gehazi exclaimed, "This is her, the very one, Whose son Elisha raised, the deed he’s done." The king heard, and justice he decreed, "Restore her land, all its fruits, fulfill her need."
Meanwhile, in Damascus, Benhadad lay weak, He heard Elisha came, and his guidance did seek. "Take gifts," said the king to his servant Hazael, "Ask the man of God if I will be well."
Hazael met Elisha with gifts galore, Forty camels burdened with treasures to implore. Elisha said, "Tell him he’ll recover and mend, But Yahweh shows me his life will soon end."
The prophet wept, his gaze locked in pain, Hazael asked, "Why these tears that fall like rain?" Elisha replied, "I see the horrors you'll bring, Fire, sword, and sorrow to Israel's offspring."
Hazael protested, "How can this be my role?" Elisha spoke true, "You'll be king, that's your goal." Hazael returned, said the king would survive, Yet the next day, his master wasn’t alive.
A cloth soaked in water ended the king's reign, Hazael took the throne, his power unchained. In Judah, Jehoram rose as king to reign, He followed Ahab’s ways, bringing shame.
Yet Yahweh spared Judah for David’s sake, A promise of a light that evil couldn't break. Edom revolted, Judah's grasp it slipped, Joram struck by night, but the bonds were ripped.
Joram's deeds were written, but he found his rest, In David's city, with his fathers, he was blessed. Ahaziah, his son, took the throne, young and bold, Following Ahab’s path, his deeds were cold.
He joined with Joram, against Syria, to fight, At Ramoth Gilead, the Syrians struck with might. Joram wounded, Ahaziah by his side, Seeking healing in Jezreel, their fates collide.
Elisha called a young prophet near, he said, "Buckle up, it's time to hear. Take this oil in your hand, get ready to ride, to Ramoth Gilead where Jehu must abide.
